test.statistic: bimodality_bc
test.threshold: BC > 0.555 required to confirm bimodal H1; BC <= 0.555 refutes H1

rivals.claim: Gene dispensability is graded/continuous: most genes impose small-to-moderate fitness costs when deleted, with essentiality forming a smooth spectrum rather than a sharp two-cluster split (consistent with polygenic buffering and metabolic network redundancy).
rivals.distinguishing_result: Pooled growth_rate/division_rate distribution across the panel shows BC <= 0.555 (unimodal or spread-out), with many genes landing at intermediate division_rate (0.3-0.7), not clustered at extremes.

rivals.claim: Apparent essentiality is condition-dependent rather than intrinsic to the gene: genes that look dispensable in basal glucose minimal media are actually essential under other conditions (e.g. acetate), so a single-condition panel overstates the 'non-essential' fraction.
rivals.distinguishing_result: Re-running the same gene panel under condition=acetate shows a different subset of genes crossing into the division_rate<0.2 lethal class than under basal, shifting the essential fraction and cluster membership rather than reproducing the same bimodal split.

auxiliary_assumptions: The simulator mechanistically implements the metabolic/regulatory consequences of each listed gene's deletion (not all genes in the panel may be wired into the model's reaction network); genes with no simulated effect will show relative growth_rate ~1 and should be interpreted as 'not modeled' rather than 'confirmed non-essential', a known scope caveat.
division_rate and growth_rate over 4 generations are sufficient to reveal lethality; slower-onset defects (e.g. accumulating damage beyond generation 4) are out of scope for this test.

Seeds (n=6) capture intrinsic stochastic noise sufficient to distinguish a lethal (division_rate~0) from viable (division_rate~1) knockout; borderline conditionally-essential genes may show high seed-to-seed variance that is treated as part of the pooled distribution, not excluded.

The bimodality coefficient is computed on pooled per-seed values across genes (treating each gene x seed as one observation), which is an appropriate operationalization of 'distribution across the gene panel' at this scale (16 genes x 6 seeds = 96 points).

drafts.question: Which genes can E. coli live without?
drafts.claim: Across the set of genes represented in this whole-cell model, a sizeable minority are individually dispensable: knocking each out one at a time leaves division_rate and growth_rate close to wildtype, while the rest are essential (division collapses). Concretely, I predict roughly 30-50% of a broad sample of tested genes are 'dispensable' (division_rate >= 0.8x wildtype and growth_rate within 20% of wildtype by generation 3), distributed non-uniformly across functional categories (e.g. central metabolism/translation genes skew essential, biosynthetic-periphery/transport genes skew dispensable).
drafts.h1: In a broad screen of single-gene knockouts (sampled across functional categories: central metabolism, translation/ribosome, amino-acid biosynthesis, transport, regulatory), the fraction classified dispensable (division_rate >= 0.8 * wildtype AND growth_rate within 20% of wildtype at generation 3, basal condition) is between 0.3 and 0.5, i.e. essentiality is bimodal-ish across genes rather than all genes being essential or all dispensable.
drafts.h0: Essentiality shows no detectable structure in this screen: the dispensable fraction is not reliably different from a floor/ceiling extreme (e.g. <10% or >90% of knockouts are dispensable), OR individual knockout division_rate/growth_rate values do not differ from wildtype beyond replicate noise (Welch |t|<2) for the great majority of tested genes, making a 'which genes' distributional claim unsupported by this sim's resolution.

operational_defs.observable: division_rate and growth_rate under single gene_knockout vs wildtype/basal
operational_defs.measure: division_rate ratio (KO/wildtype) and growth_rate ratio (KO/wildtype) averaged across seeds at generation 3

operational_defs.observable: division_rate channel >= 0.8x wildtype AND growth_rate channel within +/-20% of wildtype
operational_defs.measure: binary classification per gene per seed, then fraction of seeds/genes meeting threshold

operational_defs.observable: division_rate channel < 0.8x wildtype (division collapse) or growth_rate < 0.8x wildtype
operational_defs.measure: binary classification, complement of dispensable

operational_defs.observable: dispensable fraction computed separately per gene category (metabolism, translation, biosynthesis, transport, regulatory)
operational_defs.measure: per-category fraction dispensable compared across categories

drafts.predicted_effect: 30-50% of a ~20-gene broad sample (4-5 genes per functional category x 4-5 categories) classified dispensable by the division_rate/growth_rate threshold; translation/ribosome and central carbon metabolism genes predicted essential fraction ~80-100% (dispensable fraction <20%), while transport and amino-acid-biosynthesis-periphery genes predicted dispensable fraction ~50-70%. Overall screen-wide dispensable fraction distribution is non-uniform across categories (not a flat ~40% everywhere).

falsifier.decision_rule: Benjamini-Hochberg FDR correction (q<0.10) applied to per-gene Welch t-tests of division_rate (KO vs wildtype) across the full ~20-gene panel; require n_significant_fdr10 (genes with reliably reduced division_rate, i.e. essential) to be in a range consistent with 50-70% essential (30-50% dispensable) rather than ~0% or ~100%
falsifier.refuting_result: n_significant_fdr10 for division_rate reduction falls outside the 50-70% essential band (e.g. <=10% of genes show significant division defects, implying near-universal dispensability, OR >=90% show defects, implying near-universal essentiality), contradicting the predicted 30-50% dispensable fraction

test.statistic: per-gene Welch t of division_rate (KO vs wildtype), BH-FDR corrected across the panel
test.threshold: q<0.10; refute predicted fraction if n_significant_fdr10/n_genes falls outside [0.5,0.7] essential (i.e. outside [0.3,0.5] dispensable)

rivals.claim: Essentiality is driven mainly by ribosome/translation capacity loss (rrna operon dosage), not by loss of individual peripheral genes per se — i.e. any gene whose knockout happens to perturb ribosome_conc/ppgpp_conc substantially will appear essential regardless of its annotated function, confounding the category-based skew.
rivals.distinguishing_result: An rrna_operon_knockout control (reducing ribosome capacity directly) produces a division_rate collapse comparable to or larger than the 'essential' single-gene KOs, while ribosome_conc tracks the division defect tightly across both the rrna_operon_knockout and the translation-category single KOs, suggesting the single-gene essentiality calls are really a proxy for ribosome capacity loss rather than category-specific gene function.

rivals.claim: This model does not actually simulate most gene functions mechanistically (many genes are not wired to phenotype), so apparent 'dispensability' mostly reflects which genes the model implements rather than true biological essentiality — nearly all KOs will look like wildtype (dispensable) because the knockout has no simulated consequence.
rivals.distinguishing_result: The observed dispensable fraction is far above 50% (approaching ~90-100%) with division_rate and growth_rate Welch t-tests showing |t|<2 vs wildtype for nearly every gene in the panel, indicating a ceiling effect from unmodeled gene function rather than genuine biological dispensability.

auxiliary_assumptions: Gene-function category assignments (translation, metabolism, biosynthesis, transport) reflect the panel chosen and are a reasonable proxy for E. coli functional classes even though the simulator's own gene-to-phenotype wiring may not match real biology gene-for-gene.

division_rate and growth_rate at generation 3 are adequate proxies for essentiality; a KO that only manifests a defect after generation 4+ (slow starvation death) would be misclassified as dispensable here — acknowledged as a scope limitation of the 1-4 generation window.

Whether a given knocked-out gene is mechanistically represented in the model (vs a no-op deletion) cannot be verified a priori; genes with no simulated consequence will trivially appear dispensable, which is treated as an auxiliary caveat rather than chased further.
Seeds (n=6) capture intrinsic stochastic noise sufficient to compute Welch t and BH-FDR across the panel; systematic (non-stochastic) model misspecification is out of scope for this test.

drafts.question: Which genes can E. coli live without?
drafts.claim: Across a broad panel of non-essential-annotated E. coli genes, most single-gene knockouts are dispensable for viability under basal minimal media: the majority will show division_rate and growth_rate statistically indistinguishable from wildtype, while only a minority (candidates enriched for core biosynthetic/ribosomal functions) will show a severe growth/division defect.
drafts.h1: When screened across a panel of single-gene knockouts on basal minimal media, the fraction of knockouts with division_rate >= 0.9x wildtype and growth_rate within a small effect size of wildtype (i.e., 'viable/dispensable') is high (predicted ~70-80% of the screened panel), while a minority (~20-30%) show severe growth_rate and/or division_rate collapse (effect size large, Welch |t|>=2 vs wildtype).
drafts.h0: Gene dispensability is uniformly distributed / most knockouts are NOT dispensable: the fraction of panel genes showing wildtype-like growth_rate and division_rate is <=50%, i.e. knockouts are as likely to be lethal/severely impaired as benign, with no clear majority-dispensable pattern.

operational_defs.observable: division_rate channel (fraction of generations that divide) and growth_rate channel, measured over simulated generations after single-gene knockout
operational_defs.measure: per-seed division_rate and growth_rate averaged over seeds; a gene is classified 'dispensable' if division_rate >= 0.9 and growth_rate effect_pct vs wildtype/basal is small (|effect_pct|<20%) and Welch |t|<2; classified 'essential/severely impaired' if division_rate drops substantially or growth_rate Welch |t|>=2 with large negative effect_pct

operational_defs.observable: growth_rate and division_rate relative to wildtype/basal reference
operational_defs.measure: Welch t-test effect size and percent effect from disconfirm(target, reference, channel) across the gene panel

operational_defs.observable: distribution of per-gene classification outcomes (dispensable vs essential) across the knockout panel
operational_defs.measure: fraction of genes in panel classified dispensable, compared against the null fraction of 50%

drafts.predicted_effect: Across a panel of ~12 single-gene knockouts (mix of expected-nonessential metabolic/regulatory genes and expected-essential ribosomal/core genes), ~70-80% will be classified dispensable (division_rate>=0.9x WT, growth_rate |effect_pct|<20%, Welch|t|<2 vs wildtype/basal), and ~20-30% will show severe defects (growth_rate effect_pct <= -40%, division_rate < 0.5, Welch|t|>=2). This is a distributional/fractional claim, not a single-gene claim.

falsifier.decision_rule: For each of the panel genes (tested as individual gene_knockout designs vs wildtype/basal), run welch_disconfirm on growth_rate and division_rate; classify each gene dispensable/essential per the operational threshold (|t|<2 and division_rate>=0.9 => dispensable). Compute the fraction dispensable across the panel. Reject H1 if the dispensable fraction is <=50% (consistent with H0) rather than the predicted ~70-80%.
falsifier.refuting_result: Panel-wide dispensable fraction falls at or below 50% (i.e., half or more of screened genes show Welch |t|>=2 drop in growth_rate or division_rate<0.9), indicating dispensability is not the majority pattern.

test.statistic: welch_t on growth_rate and division_rate, per gene vs wildtype/basal; then fraction dispensable across panel compared to 50% threshold
test.threshold: dispensable fraction >50% required to support H1; |t|>=2 defines 'essential/impaired' per gene

rivals.claim: Rival A: Dispensability is bimodal but driven primarily by functional category (ribosomal/core genes near-universally essential, metabolic/regulatory genes near-universally dispensable) rather than being a smooth majority/minority split — i.e. the panel result would show two sharp clusters at the extremes with few intermediate phenotypes.
rivals.distinguishing_result: bimodality_bc on the pooled per-gene growth_rate effect sizes across the panel yields BC>0.555, indicating a bimodal (two-cluster) distribution rather than a single dispensable-majority mode with a few extreme outliers.

rivals.claim: Rival B: Many 'dispensable' genes are only conditionally dispensable because basal minimal media masks a ppGpp/stringent-response-mediated compensation that rescues growth; removing that compensatory capacity (e.g., via rrna_operon_knockout reducing ribosome buffer, or clamping ppgpp_conc) would reveal many more genes as essential, meaning the measured dispensability fraction is an artifact of a single permissive condition, not a general property of the genes.
rivals.distinguishing_result: When the same panel subset is re-tested under rrna_operon_knockout (reduced ribosome capacity) as background, a substantial subset of genes previously classified dispensable now show division_rate<0.9 or Welch|t|>=2 growth_rate drop, showing the WT dispensable fraction was condition-dependent rather than intrinsic.

auxiliary_assumptions: Whether a given gene's knockout is mechanistically simulated (i.e., the model encodes a functional consequence for that gene) is not knowable in advance; genes with no simulated phenotype will trivially register as 'dispensable' and this is treated as a scope caveat, not a confound to resolve here.
division_rate and growth_rate are read at the same simulated generation windows across all designs so comparisons are time-matched.

The panel of 12 genes is treated as a representative (not exhaustive) sample of the genome for the purposes of this screen; generalizing the fraction to 'the genome' rides on this sample being reasonably diverse (core/essential vs peripheral/metabolic genes).
Basal minimal media is the single condition tested; dispensability is scoped to this condition only (per Rival B), not claimed as condition-invariant.

Stochastic seed-to-seed variation (intrinsic noise) is assumed small enough relative to knockout effect sizes that 6 seeds give adequate power to distinguish dispensable vs essential phenotypes at the stated thresholds.

drafts.question: Which genes can E. coli live without?
drafts.claim: Among a broad panel of individually non-essential genes (classically defined as genes whose single knockout permits colony formation in rich media), the majority cause little or no growth-rate decrement in this simulator, but a nontrivial minority (roughly 10-20%) produce a measurable growth or division defect (>=15% reduction in growth_rate or division_rate <1) despite being formally 'viable' — i.e. 'can live without' is not binary but a graded distribution of fitness costs, and most of the panel will cluster near zero effect while a distinguishable tail shows partial defects.
drafts.h1: For a panel of >=15 genes annotated non-essential in E. coli (e.g. acrB, araA, dps, cspA, yciI, ompF, fliC, flgK, treA, gatY, nanA, mglB, rbsK, puuA, ygfZ), knockout growth_rate and division_rate across seeds will show a distribution with a mode near zero effect (|Δgrowth_rate| < 10% of wildtype) but a tail of >=10% of genes showing >=15% growth_rate reduction and/or division_rate < 1, detected via FDR-corrected per-gene comparisons against wildtype.
drafts.h0: All (or nearly all, <5%) of the panel genes show no significant growth_rate or division_rate difference from wildtype/basal after FDR correction — i.e. the simulator treats 'non-essential' genes as uniformly neutral with no distinguishable fitness tail.

operational_defs.observable: division_rate
operational_defs.measure: fraction of simulated generations that complete division; division_rate < 1 flags a lethality or severe division defect

operational_defs.observable: growth_rate
operational_defs.measure: percent change in instantaneous specific growth rate (1/h) of knockout vs wildtype/basal, averaged across seeds

operational_defs.construct: distribution shape across the gene panel
operational_defs.observable: growth_rate, division_rate (per-gene, per-seed)
operational_defs.measure: per-gene log2 fold-change in growth_rate vs wildtype, aggregated across the panel; fraction of genes exceeding a 15% reduction threshold after BH-FDR correction

drafts.predicted_effect: Distribution form: right-skewed/long-tailed fitness-cost distribution. Predicted ~80-90% of the 15-20 gene panel show |Δgrowth_rate| < 10% (near-neutral mode), while ~10-20% (i.e. 2-4 of 15-20 genes) show growth_rate reduction >=15% and/or division_rate < 1, surviving BH-FDR at q<0.10.

falsifier.decision_rule: For each of the >=15 knockout genes, run Welch's t-test of growth_rate (seed-level) vs wildtype/basal; collect per-gene p-values and effect_pct, apply Benjamini-Hochberg FDR correction (q<0.10). Reject H1 if n_significant_fdr10 == 0 (no gene shows a detectable defect) OR if n_significant_fdr10 / n_tested > 0.5 (defect is the rule, not a minority tail), either of which contradicts the predicted ~10-20% tail.
falsifier.refuting_result: Either zero genes pass FDR<0.10 with >=15% growth_rate reduction (panel uniformly neutral, supporting H0), or more than half the panel shows such defects (panel is NOT mostly dispensable, contradicting the 'non-essential' framing entirely).

test.statistic: per-gene Welch t -> BH-FDR corrected q-value on growth_rate log2FC vs wildtype
test.threshold: q<0.10 AND |effect_pct|>=15% defines a 'mover'; reject H1 if n_significant_fdr10==0 or >50% of panel

rivals.claim: Rival A: Knockout effects are essentially binary (lethal vs fully neutral) with no graded intermediate tail — the simulator's metabolic/regulatory network either has full redundancy (no effect) or no redundancy (crash), so no 10-20% partial-defect tail exists.
rivals.distinguishing_result: If true, the per-gene effect_pct distribution would be bimodal at the extremes (near 0% and near -100%/division failure) with almost nothing in the 15-50% intermediate range; bimodality_bc on pooled effect_pct would exceed 0.555 with modes at the extremes rather than a long right tail.

rivals.claim: Rival B: Any observed 'defect tail' is driven by generic growth-rate noise/variance across seeds rather than a reproducible gene-specific cost — i.e. apparent movers are false positives from seed-to-seed stochasticity, not real fitness effects.
rivals.distinguishing_result: If true, the per-gene seed replicates would show high within-gene variance comparable to between-gene variance, and re-running with more seeds would fail to reproduce which specific genes pass FDR (the significant gene set would be unstable/incoherent across seed subsets), unlike a genuine gene-specific tail that is stable and interpretable (e.g. clustering around transport/ribosome-adjacent genes).

auxiliary_assumptions: The simulator mechanistically implements the metabolic/regulatory consequences of each knocked-out gene (not all genes in the panel may be wired into the model; genes with no simulated mechanism will trivially show zero effect, which is a model-coverage caveat, not evidence of true neutrality).
Growth_rate and division_rate at 3 generations are sufficient to detect a steady-state fitness defect (a slower-manifesting defect beyond gen 3-4 would be missed).

Gene panel selection (classically non-essential genes spanning transport, stress response, catabolism, motility) is representative of the broader non-essential gene space, not cherry-picked toward neutrality or toward known redundancy loss.
Basal media condition is the appropriate condition for testing baseline dispensability; some genes may only show cost under alternative conditions (e.g. acetate), which is out of scope for this test.

Seed count of 6 provides adequate replicate power for Welch's t per gene at this effect size; true effects near the 15% threshold may require more seeds for full power (addressed only qualitatively, not via explicit power_mde here).

params.note: interventional control: capacity-limiting background perturbation to compare defect magnitude/mechanism against a known ribosome-limitation phenotype, distinguishing generic capacity loss from gene-specific redundancy loss

drafts.question: Which genes can E. coli live without?
drafts.claim: A substantial minority of individually-deleted non-essential-looking genes (drawn from a panel of weakly-expressed/paralogous/accessory metabolic genes) are dispensable for growth on basal minimal media: across a screen of single-gene knockouts, roughly 60-80% will show no detectable growth defect (division_rate and growth_rate statistically indistinguishable from wildtype), while the remainder show partial or full lethality.
drafts.h1: For the sampled panel of candidate genes, the fraction of single-gene knockouts that are 'viable' (division_rate >= 0.8x wildtype AND growth_rate Welch |t| < 2 vs wildtype) is >= 0.5, i.e. E. coli can live without most of these genes individually.
drafts.h0: The fraction of viable knockouts in the panel is < 0.5 (i.e. most single-gene deletions in the panel are lethal or strongly growth-impairing), OR there is no distinguishable sub-population — all knockouts show similar growth_rate/division_rate reductions relative to wildtype (unimodal, not bimodal, distribution of per-gene effect sizes).

operational_defs.observable: division_rate and growth_rate channels for a gene_knockout design vs wildtype/basal reference
operational_defs.measure: per-seed division_rate (fraction of generations dividing) and growth_rate (1/h); a gene is scored 'viable' if division_rate >= 0.8 and Welch |t| for growth_rate vs reference is < 2

operational_defs.observable: distribution across the gene panel of per-gene effect_pct (growth_rate relative to wildtype) and division_rate
operational_defs.measure: fraction of genes classified viable by the threshold above; bimodality coefficient of the pooled per-gene growth_rate effect sizes

drafts.predicted_effect: Bimodal distribution of per-gene growth effects: predicted viable fraction ~0.65 (65% of panel genes show growth_rate effect_pct within +/-10% of wildtype and division_rate>=0.8), remaining ~35% show growth_rate reduction >50% or division_rate<0.5. Sarle's bimodality coefficient BC > 0.555 over pooled per-gene growth_rate effect sizes.

falsifier.decision_rule: Step 1 (screen): for each of the 12 panel genes, run welch_disconfirm on growth_rate (gene_knockout/basal vs wildtype/basal, seeds pooled); classify viable if |t|<2 AND division_rate>=0.8x reference mean. Compute viable_fraction across the 12-gene panel; H1 requires viable_fraction>=0.5. Step 2 (shape): compute Sarle's bimodality coefficient (bimodality_bc) over the pooled per-gene growth_rate effect_pct values; reject unimodal-null if BC>0.555.
falsifier.refuting_result: viable_fraction < 0.5 across the panel, OR BC <= 0.555 (effects form a single smeared distribution rather than a bimodal viable/lethal split) — this would refute the claim that most sampled genes are individually dispensable with a clean bimodal split.

test.statistic: Sarle's bimodality coefficient over pooled per-gene growth_rate effect_pct (log2FC-style), supplemented by per-gene welch_disconfirm classification
test.threshold: BC>0.555 for bimodal shape; viable_fraction>=0.5 for the magnitude claim

rivals.claim: Rival A: essentiality is NOT a clean bimodal viable/lethal split but a graded continuum (many genes cause intermediate growth slowdowns rather than full lethality or full viability) reflecting polygenic metabolic buffering.
rivals.distinguishing_result: bimodality_bc returns BC<=0.555 and per-gene effect_pct values are spread continuously across the range rather than clustering near 0% and near -100%.

rivals.claim: Rival B: apparent dispensability is an artifact of incomplete pathway simulation — genes the model does not mechanistically wire into growth-limiting reactions will trivially show no phenotype regardless of true biological essentiality, inflating the viable_fraction.
rivals.distinguishing_result: a control panel of genes KNOWN to be essential in vivo (e.g. core ribosomal protein genes) also shows division_rate>=0.8 and |t|<2 in this simulator, indicating the viable classification reflects simulator coverage gaps rather than true dispensability.

auxiliary_assumptions: The simulator's mechanistic wiring for these 12 panel genes is sufficient to produce a growth phenotype when one exists in vivo (checked downstream, not resolvable here).

Seeds (6) and generations (3) give adequate replicate power to distinguish |t|>=2 from noise for genes with large true effects; genuinely marginal/intermediate-effect genes may require more seeds (a scope caveat, not something the sim design itself can fix).
Panel genes were chosen a priori as plausible non-essential/paralogous/weakly-expressed candidates based on known E. coli biology, not resampled post hoc from the simulation's own results.
division_rate and growth_rate are treated as the operational proxies for 'can live without'; subtler fitness costs (e.g. stress sensitivity not captured by these channels) are out of scope.

drafts.question: Which genes can E. coli live without?
drafts.claim: Across a broad screen of single-gene knockouts in E. coli grown on basal minimal medium, most genes are individually dispensable: roughly 80% of tested non-essential-looking genes will show near-wildtype growth rate and division rate, while a minority (~20%) will show a severe growth/division defect (viability-reducing) phenotype, consistent with known genome-wide essentiality fractions (~5-10% essential in rich media, higher in minimal media).
drafts.h1: In a panel of single-gene knockouts spanning diverse functional categories (biosynthesis, transport, regulatory, stress-response), the DISTRIBUTION of growth-rate and division-rate effects is bimodal: a dispensable majority clusters near wildtype levels, and an essential/near-essential minority clusters at severely reduced growth/division rate, with the minority fraction in the ~15-30% range on minimal (basal) medium.
drafts.h0: Knockout effects on growth_rate and division_rate are unimodally distributed around a single reduced mean (no distinct dispensable/essential clustering), i.e. gene loss produces a continuous graded fitness cost with no bimodal split, OR the dispensable fraction is <50% (most genes are NOT individually dispensable) on minimal medium.

operational_defs.observable: growth_rate and division_rate of a single-gene knockout relative to wildtype/basal
operational_defs.measure: per-seed growth_rate (1/h) and division_rate (frac) averaged over generations 2-4, normalized to wildtype mean

operational_defs.observable: normalized growth_rate/division_rate value per knockout averaged across seeds
operational_defs.measure: threshold: knockout classified 'severe/essential-like' if division_rate < 0.5 of wildtype OR growth_rate < 0.5 of wildtype; else 'dispensable'

operational_defs.observable: pooled per-gene normalized growth_rate values across the screened gene panel
operational_defs.measure: Sarle's bimodality coefficient (BC) computed over pooled normalized growth_rate across all knocked-out genes and seeds

drafts.predicted_effect: Bimodal distribution of normalized growth_rate across the gene panel with BC>0.555; dispensable cluster centered near 1.0 (within 10%) comprising ~70-85% of genes, essential/severe cluster centered <=0.5 comprising ~15-30% of genes; aggregate panel-wide mean growth_rate reduction modest (~10-15% below wildtype) because the majority of genes are dispensable.

falsifier.decision_rule: Compute Sarle's bimodality coefficient (bimodality_bc) over pooled per-seed, per-gene normalized growth_rate values across the full knockout panel (>=20 genes x 4 seeds). Reject H1 (no bimodal essential/dispensable split) if BC<=0.555. Separately, classify each knockout as essential-like (division_rate<0.5x wildtype) vs dispensable; reject H1 if the dispensable fraction is <50% (binomial check against 50% using the proportion CI from BH-FDR mover count).
falsifier.refuting_result: BC<=0.555 (unimodal/continuous distribution of fitness effects) and/or dispensable fraction <50%, indicating gene loss produces a graded continuum rather than a bimodal essential/dispensable split, or that most sampled genes are NOT dispensable on minimal medium.

test.statistic: Sarle's bimodality coefficient (BC) over pooled normalized growth_rate across the knockout panel
test.threshold: BC>0.555 for bimodal; else reject H1

rivals.claim: Rival A (graded continuum): gene dispensability is not bimodal but forms a continuous gradient of fitness costs (many genes give intermediate ~20-70% growth reductions), because metabolic network flux rerouting produces smooth, dose-dependent fitness penalties rather than a sharp essential/non-essential split.
rivals.distinguishing_result: Pooled normalized growth_rate histogram shows a broad unimodal or multimodal-but-not-bimodal shape (BC<=0.555) with substantial density at intermediate values (0.5-0.9), rather than two separated clusters near 1.0 and <=0.5.

rivals.claim: Rival B (media-dependence confound): the apparent dispensable/essential split is an artifact of testing only on basal minimal medium; many 'dispensable' genes on basal would actually be essential on a different condition (e.g. acetate), so the dispensability fraction is not a fixed property of the gene but of the gene-by-media interaction, and the basal-only screen overestimates the dispensable fraction.
rivals.distinguishing_result: Running the same knockout panel on an alternative static condition (e.g. acetate) shows a substantially different (e.g. >15 percentage point lower) dispensable fraction and a different set of genes classified essential, indicating condition-dependence rather than an intrinsic bimodal gene property.

auxiliary_assumptions: The simulator mechanistically implements the metabolic/regulatory consequences of each knocked-out gene (not all gene deletions may have a coded phenotype; genes with no simulated effect will trivially appear 'dispensable', which is a model-coverage limitation, not a biological claim, and is recorded as a scope caveat).
Growth_rate and division_rate averaged over generations 2-4 (excluding generation 1 startup transient) are adequate summaries of steady-state fitness for each knockout.

The 20-gene panel (mix of biosynthesis, central metabolism, and a non-essential control like acrB) is treated as a representative sample of the genome-wide essentiality distribution; true genome-wide inference would require a much larger panel, acknowledged as a scope limitation of this modest-scale screen.
Classifying 'essential-like' via division_rate<0.5x wildtype is a fixed operational threshold; genes with intermediate phenotypes (0.5-0.8x) are a known gray zone not resolved by this binary cut.
Seeds=4 per knockout is assumed sufficient to estimate per-gene mean growth_rate for pooling into the panel-wide bimodality test; individual gene-level significance is not separately powered.

drafts.question: Which genes can E. coli live without?
drafts.claim: Across a broad panel of single non-essential-annotated genes, most single-gene knockouts (a majority, roughly 70-90%) are individually dispensable for growth in basal minimal medium — cells survive and divide, though many show a measurable (10-40%) growth-rate penalty — while a minority (~10-30%) are conditionally or absolutely essential, showing near-zero division_rate and collapsed growth_rate.
drafts.h1: In basal minimal medium, the distribution of single-gene-knockout phenotypes across a diverse gene panel is bimodal: a dispensable majority (division_rate ~1, growth_rate reduced but >0) and an essential minority (division_rate ~0, growth_rate collapsed), with the essential fraction falling roughly between 10% and 30% of the sampled panel.
drafts.h0: Single-gene knockouts across the panel do not separate into dispensable/essential modes; division_rate and growth_rate are unimodally and continuously distributed around the wildtype reference with no distinct near-zero cluster, i.e. gene loss produces a smooth graded effect rather than a bimodal essential/non-essential split.

operational_defs.observable: division_rate
operational_defs.measure: fraction of simulated generations that complete division over 4 generations, per seed, per knockout

operational_defs.observable: growth_rate
operational_defs.measure: mean instantaneous specific growth rate (1/h) across seeds relative to wildtype/basal mean

operational_defs.observable: division_rate distribution across the gene panel
operational_defs.measure: Sarle's bimodality coefficient (BC) over pooled per-seed division_rate values across all knocked-out genes; genes with division_rate<0.2 classified essential, >=0.8 classified dispensable

drafts.predicted_effect: Bimodal distribution of division_rate across a panel of ~15-20 single-gene knockouts: BC>0.555 (target ~0.6-0.7), with an essential-mode fraction of 10-30% of genes (division_rate<0.2) and a dispensable-mode fraction of 70-90% (division_rate>=0.8, growth_rate reduced by 10-40% vs wildtype on average within that mode).

falsifier.decision_rule: Compute Sarle's bimodality coefficient (BC) over pooled per-seed division_rate values across the full gene panel (~15-20 genes x 6 seeds). Reject H0 (unimodal) if BC>0.555. Additionally, require the low-division_rate cluster to comprise between 10% and 30% of genes; if BC<=0.555 or the essential fraction falls outside [5%,40%], H1 is refuted.
falsifier.refuting_result: BC<=0.555 (division_rate values form a single continuous cluster with no distinct near-zero mode), OR the fraction of genes classified essential is <5% (almost nothing is essential) or >40% (far more genes essential than expected), indicating the panel does not show a clean dispensable/essential split.

test.statistic: Sarle's bimodality coefficient (BC) on pooled per-seed division_rate across gene panel
test.threshold: BC>0.555 for bimodal rejection of H0; essential fraction in [10%,30%] (tolerance [5%,40%]) for H1 support

rivals.claim: Graded-essentiality rival: gene loss produces a continuous spectrum of fitness costs (no sharp essential/dispensable split) because most genes contribute partial, additive flux/capacity rather than being binary switches.
rivals.distinguishing_result: division_rate and growth_rate values across the panel form a single broad unimodal distribution (BC<=0.555) with genes spread continuously from near-wildtype to near-zero, rather than clustering into two separable modes.

rivals.claim: Media-dependence rival: apparent 'essentiality' in this test is an artifact of the single basal condition; genes scored essential here would be dispensable under a richer condition (e.g. amino-acid-supplemented), so the bimodal split reflects condition-specific auxotrophy rather than true indispensability.
rivals.distinguishing_result: Running the same KO panel under a condition/timeline with amino-acid supplementation shifts genes from the essential (division_rate<0.2) cluster into the dispensable cluster (division_rate>=0.8), shrinking the essential fraction substantially versus basal.

select_score.question: Which genes can E. coli live without?
select_score.claim: Across a broad panel of single-gene knockouts, a substantial minority (~20-30%) are effectively dispensable for growth on basal minimal medium: their deletion yields a growth rate and division rate statistically indistinguishable from wildtype (within ~10% of wildtype growth_rate), while the rest show a significant growth/division defect, consistent with known E. coli essentiality screens (~87-93% of genes nonessential genome-wide, but with heterogeneous fitness costs among the 'nonessential' set tested here).
select_score.h1: When a panel of single-gene knockouts is simulated on basal minimal medium, the per-gene distribution of growth-rate effect sizes (KO vs wildtype) is bimodal: one cluster near zero effect (dispensable genes, predicted ~20-30% of the panel) and one cluster with strong negative effect (conditionally essential/essential-like genes), rather than a single unimodal distribution of mild, uniformly small defects.
select_score.h0: Growth-rate and division-rate effects of single-gene knockouts across the panel are unimodally and continuously distributed around a single mean defect (no distinct dispensable cluster separable from a defective cluster), i.e. unimodal with Sarle's bimodality coefficient <=0.555, and/or the fraction of knockouts statistically indistinguishable from wildtype is not detectably different from 0.

operational_defs.observable: growth_rate and division_rate of a gene_knockout design vs wildtype/basal reference, across seeds
operational_defs.measure: Welch t-test per gene (KO vs WT) on growth_rate; gene classified 'dispensable' if |welch_t|<2 AND division_rate within 0.95-1.0 of WT; else 'costly'

operational_defs.observable: per-gene effect_pct (percent growth-rate change KO vs WT) pooled across the gene panel
operational_defs.measure: Sarle's bimodality coefficient over the pooled per-gene effect_pct values

operational_defs.observable: count of genes classified dispensable (per Welch test) divided by panel size
operational_defs.measure: BH-FDR-corrected proportion test across the panel; report fraction with 95% CI

select_score.predicted_effect: Bimodal distribution of per-gene growth-rate effect_pct with bimodality coefficient BC>0.555; dispensable cluster centered near 0% change (within +/-10%), costly cluster centered at <= -40% change; predicted fraction dispensable ~20-30% of a ~20-30 gene panel spanning metabolic, biosynthetic, transport, and regulatory categories.

falsifier.decision_rule: Compute Sarle's bimodality coefficient over the pooled per-gene effect_pct distribution from the panel; reject H1 (bimodal dispensable/costly structure) if BC<=0.555 (unimodal). Separately, for each gene run Welch t of growth_rate (KO vs WT) across seeds with BH-FDR correction at q<0.10 across the panel; reject H1 if the fraction of genes classified dispensable (|welch_t|<2 and division_rate>=0.95) is not detectably different from 0 (i.e., fewer than ~2 of ~25 genes qualify).
falsifier.refuting_result: Pooled effect_pct distribution is unimodal (BC<=0.555) and/or fewer than ~8% of panel genes qualify as dispensable, indicating knockout effects form a single continuous distribution of costs rather than a distinct dispensable subpopulation.

test.statistic: Sarle's bimodality coefficient (BC) over pooled per-gene effect_pct; secondary bh_fdr_movers over per-gene welch_t for fraction-dispensable test
test.threshold: BC>0.555 for bimodal; fraction dispensable 95% CI must exclude 0 and include values >=15%

rivals.claim: Rival A: Dispensability is not bimodal but a smooth continuum of fitness costs (polygenic buffering), so no sharp dispensable cluster exists — the apparent WT-like genes are just the low tail of a single unimodal cost distribution.
rivals.distinguishing_result: Pooled effect_pct distribution shows BC<=0.555 (unimodal) even though some genes individually pass the |welch_t|<2 threshold — the 'dispensable' genes are statistically indistinguishable from a continuous tail, not a separate mode.

rivals.claim: Rival B: Apparent dispensability is an artifact of insufficient simulated time/generations — genes classified dispensable at 2-4 generations would show defects if run longer (slow-growth lethality), so true essential fraction is underestimated.
rivals.distinguishing_result: Re-running the same 'dispensable' subset at an extended generation count (e.g. via a timeline with prolonged basal exposure) reveals division_rate dropping below 0.95 or growth_rate declining >10% that was not visible at 2-4 generations, i.e. the dispensable/costly boundary is generation-count-dependent rather than a stable structural feature.

hypothesis.question: Which genes can E. coli live without?
hypothesis.claim: Across a broad screen of single-gene knockouts in E. coli grown on basal minimal medium, most genes are individually dispensable: roughly 80% of tested non-essential-looking genes will show near-wildtype growth rate and division rate, while a minority (~20%) will show a severe growth/division defect (viability-reducing) phenotype, consistent with known genome-wide essentiality fractions (~5-10% essential in rich media, higher in minimal media).
hypothesis.h1: In a panel of single-gene knockouts spanning diverse functional categories (biosynthesis, transport, regulatory, stress-response), the DISTRIBUTION of growth-rate and division-rate effects is bimodal: a dispensable majority clusters near wildtype levels, and an essential/near-essential minority clusters at severely reduced growth/division rate, with the minority fraction in the ~15-30% range on minimal (basal) medium.
hypothesis.h0: Knockout effects on growth_rate and division_rate are unimodally distributed around a single reduced mean (no distinct dispensable/essential clustering), i.e. gene loss produces a continuous graded fitness cost with no bimodal split, OR the dispensable fraction is <50% (most genes are NOT individually dispensable) on minimal medium.

operational_defs.observable: growth_rate and division_rate of a single-gene knockout relative to wildtype/basal
operational_defs.measure: per-seed growth_rate (1/h) and division_rate (frac) averaged over generations 2-4, normalized to wildtype mean

operational_defs.observable: normalized growth_rate/division_rate value per knockout averaged across seeds
operational_defs.measure: threshold: knockout classified 'severe/essential-like' if division_rate < 0.5 of wildtype OR growth_rate < 0.5 of wildtype; else 'dispensable'

operational_defs.observable: pooled per-gene normalized growth_rate values across the screened gene panel
operational_defs.measure: Sarle's bimodality coefficient (BC) computed over pooled normalized growth_rate across all knocked-out genes and seeds

hypothesis.predicted_effect: Bimodal distribution of normalized growth_rate across the gene panel with BC>0.555; dispensable cluster centered near 1.0 (within 10%) comprising ~70-85% of genes, essential/severe cluster centered <=0.5 comprising ~15-30% of genes; aggregate panel-wide mean growth_rate reduction modest (~10-15% below wildtype) because the majority of genes are dispensable.

falsifier.decision_rule: Compute Sarle's bimodality coefficient (bimodality_bc) over pooled per-seed, per-gene normalized growth_rate values across the full knockout panel (>=20 genes x 4 seeds). Reject H1 (no bimodal essential/dispensable split) if BC<=0.555. Separately, classify each knockout as essential-like (division_rate<0.5x wildtype) vs dispensable; reject H1 if the dispensable fraction is <50% (binomial check against 50% using the proportion CI from BH-FDR mover count).
falsifier.refuting_result: BC<=0.555 (unimodal/continuous distribution of fitness effects) and/or dispensable fraction <50%, indicating gene loss produces a graded continuum rather than a bimodal essential/dispensable split, or that most sampled genes are NOT dispensable on minimal medium.

test.statistic: Sarle's bimodality coefficient (BC) over pooled normalized growth_rate across the knockout panel
test.threshold: BC>0.555 for bimodal; else reject H1

rivals.claim: Rival A (graded continuum): gene dispensability is not bimodal but forms a continuous gradient of fitness costs (many genes give intermediate ~20-70% growth reductions), because metabolic network flux rerouting produces smooth, dose-dependent fitness penalties rather than a sharp essential/non-essential split.
rivals.distinguishing_result: Pooled normalized growth_rate histogram shows a broad unimodal or multimodal-but-not-bimodal shape (BC<=0.555) with substantial density at intermediate values (0.5-0.9), rather than two separated clusters near 1.0 and <=0.5.

rivals.claim: Rival B (media-dependence confound): the apparent dispensable/essential split is an artifact of testing only on basal minimal medium; many 'dispensable' genes on basal would actually be essential on a different condition (e.g. acetate), so the dispensability fraction is not a fixed property of the gene but of the gene-by-media interaction, and the basal-only screen overestimates the dispensable fraction.
rivals.distinguishing_result: Running the same knockout panel on an alternative static condition (e.g. acetate) shows a substantially different (e.g. >15 percentage point lower) dispensable fraction and a different set of genes classified essential, indicating condition-dependence rather than an intrinsic bimodal gene property.

auxiliary_assumptions: The simulator mechanistically implements the metabolic/regulatory consequences of each knocked-out gene (not all gene deletions may have a coded phenotype; genes with no simulated effect will trivially appear 'dispensable', which is a model-coverage limitation, not a biological claim, and is recorded as a scope caveat).
Growth_rate and division_rate averaged over generations 2-4 (excluding generation 1 startup transient) are adequate summaries of steady-state fitness for each knockout.

The 20-gene panel (mix of biosynthesis, central metabolism, and a non-essential control like acrB) is treated as a representative sample of the genome-wide essentiality distribution; true genome-wide inference would require a much larger panel, acknowledged as a scope limitation of this modest-scale screen.
Classifying 'essential-like' via division_rate<0.5x wildtype is a fixed operational threshold; genes with intermediate phenotypes (0.5-0.8x) are a known gray zone not resolved by this binary cut.
Seeds=4 per knockout is assumed sufficient to estimate per-gene mean growth_rate for pooling into the panel-wide bimodality test; individual gene-level significance is not separately powered.

hypothesis.question: How do bacteria choose between two sugars in the same flask?
hypothesis.claim: Carbon catabolite repression via the stringent/ppGpp-coupled regulatory axis forces sequential (diauxic-like) sugar use: when a preferred carbon source is available, cells suppress growth-rate-normalized capacity for the alternative sugar pathway, which should show up in this simulator as a ppGpp/ribosome-allocation signature that differs between a 'preferred-sugar' condition and an 'alternative-sugar' condition, rather than both being used simultaneously. Because the instrument's carbon uptake is a binary per-condition switch (no mid-run carbon switch, no real dual-sugar mixing), the operational proxy for 'choice' is: the steady-state physiological state (growth rate, ppGpp, ribosome allocation) under a glucose-like condition should resemble the canonical repressing state, and this state should be causally dependent on ppGpp/stringent signaling, not merely correlated with growth rate.
hypothesis.h1: Across static media conditions representing different single-sugar environments, the preferred (fast, glycolytic) condition produces a distinct, ppGpp-dependent low-stringency physiological state (lower ppgpp_conc, higher ribosome_conc, higher growth_rate) relative to a slower, less-preferred-sugar-like condition (e.g. acetate), and this difference is causally mediated by ppGpp signaling (abolished/attenuated when ppGpp synthesis is knocked out), consistent with a regulatory hierarchy that would produce sequential/exclusionary sugar use rather than co-utilization.
hypothesis.h0: The physiological state (growth_rate, ppgpp_conc, ribosome_conc) does not differ meaningfully between the glucose-like (basal) and acetate conditions beyond replicate noise, OR any observed difference persists unchanged when RelA (ppGpp synthetase) is knocked out, indicating the difference is not ppGpp-mediated.

operational_defs.construct: preference for fast/glycolytic sugar (catabolite repression state)
operational_defs.observable: growth_rate and ribosome_conc under basal (glucose-like) condition
operational_defs.measure: mean growth_rate (1/h) and ribosome_conc (uM) across seeds, wildtype/basal

operational_defs.construct: stringent response activation under less-preferred carbon source
operational_defs.observable: ppgpp_conc under acetate condition vs basal
operational_defs.measure: mean ppgpp_conc (uM) across seeds, wildtype/acetate vs wildtype/basal

operational_defs.construct: causal dependence of the repression-like state on ppGpp signaling
operational_defs.observable: ppgpp_conc and growth_rate under acetate with relA knocked out vs intact
operational_defs.measure: disconfirm(relA_knockout/acetate, wildtype/acetate, ppgpp_conc) and (growth_rate)

hypothesis.predicted_effect: Basal (glucose-like) vs acetate: growth_rate higher by >=1.5-fold (e.g. ~0.9/h vs ~0.5/h), ppgpp_conc lower by >=30% (e.g. ~20 uM vs ~30+ uM) in basal, ribosome_conc higher by >=20% in basal. In relA-knockout/acetate, the ppgpp_conc elevation seen in wildtype/acetate should be attenuated by >=50% relative to wildtype/acetate, demonstrating causal dependence on ppGpp synthesis.

falsifier.decision_rule: Welch t of ppgpp_conc, condition/acetate vs wildtype/basal, across seeds; reject H0 if two-sided |t|>=2 AND effect_pct indicates acetate ppgpp_conc is >=30% higher than basal
falsifier.refuting_result: If |t|<2 or acetate ppgpp_conc is not meaningfully elevated (<30% difference, or in the wrong direction) relative to basal, H1's claim of a distinct stringent-response signature for the less-preferred carbon source is refuted.

test.statistic: welch_t
test.threshold: |t|>=2 and effect_pct>=30%

rivals.claim: Growth-rate-dependent passive dilution: differences in ppgpp_conc and ribosome_conc between basal and acetate are simply a byproduct of different growth rates (faster growth dilutes/accumulates regulators differently), with no causal/regulatory 'choice' mechanism specific to ppGpp signaling.
rivals.distinguishing_result: If relA_knockout/acetate still shows elevated ppgpp_conc and the same growth-rate difference persists unchanged relative to wildtype/acetate (i.e., disconfirm shows no attenuation), this supports the passive-dilution rival over a causal ppGpp-mediated mechanism.

rivals.claim: Ribosome allocation alone (independent of ppGpp) drives the apparent preference signature: constraints on ribosome capacity (not ppGpp signaling) explain the growth_rate/ribosome_conc difference between conditions.
rivals.distinguishing_result: An rrna_operon_knockout/basal condition that reduces ribosome capacity should lower growth_rate similarly to the acetate condition even without changing ppgpp_conc; if growth_rate drops to acetate-like levels while ppgpp_conc stays low (basal-like), this supports ribosome-capacity-driven rather than ppGpp-driven differentiation.

auxiliary_assumptions: The simulator's binary per-condition carbon uptake (no mid-run dual-sugar mixing or glucose-dose gradient) means true simultaneous two-sugar choice/preference-switching cannot be directly staged; basal (glucose-like) vs acetate static conditions are used as proxies for 'preferred' vs 'less-preferred' carbon source physiological end-states.

acetate is treated as a representative slower/less-preferred carbon source consistent with the static_only_carbon list; its physiology is assumed to approximate the repressed/non-preferred branch of a hierarchy, not a literal second sugar in true mixed culture.

relA knockout is assumed to meaningfully attenuate ppGpp synthesis in this model (the stringent-response module); if relA's effect is not mechanistically implemented for this condition, the causal test would be uninformative rather than falsifying (a scope caveat, not resolvable within this instrument).

Growth rate, ppgpp_conc, and ribosome_conc are each assumed to be reliably computed as steady-state channels (steady-state charging regime) for both basal and acetate conditions without requiring the kinetic ppGpp module.
residual_ambiguities: [outruns_instrument] The model's 'seeds' most likely instantiate independent whole-population (bulk) simulation runs with randomized initial/parameter draws, not individual cells within one shared population. The claim is about per-cell asynchrony WITHIN a population, but the operationalization pools across seeds (separate simulation replicates), which conflates population-replicate variance with single-cell heterogeneity.

[outruns_instrument] The model's 'seeds' most likely instantiate independent whole-population (bulk) simulation runs with randomized initial/parameter draws, not individual cells within one shared population. The claim is about per-cell asynchrony WITHIN a population, but the operationalization pools across seeds (separate simulation replicates), which conflates population-replicate variance with single-cell heterogeneity.

objection_ledger.issue: The model's 'seeds' most likely instantiate independent whole-population (bulk) simulation runs with randomized initial/parameter draws, not individual cells within one shared population. The claim is about per-cell asynchrony WITHIN a population, but the operationalization pools across seeds (separate simulation replicates), which conflates population-replicate variance with single-cell heterogeneity.

The decision_rule combines a Welch t-test (designed to detect a difference in MEANS) with a claim about DISPERSION (CV, variance). A Welch t-test on 'growth_rate at a fixed post-shift timepoint' tests whether shift and basal groups have different average growth_rate, not whether the shift group is more dispersed. As written it's unclear whether |welch_t|>=2 on means is being used as a proxy for a variance claim, which could pass or fail independently of whether CV truly differs. The test for the core asynchrony claim should be a variance-comparison statistic (e.g., Levene's test or F-test on variances, or a direct CV ratio with a bootstrap CI) rather than a t-test on means.

The instrument appears to be a population-level/few-seed stochastic simulator; 'cell-to-cell heterogeneity' and 'bimodality across isogenic cells' are being operationalized as variance across 8 independent simulation seeds, not actual single-cell measurements within one population. This is a real gap between the claim (within-population single-cell asynchrony) and what 8 seeds of a possibly deterministic-per-seed model can show, but the candidate already flags this as an explicit auxiliary assumption.

The user's question is about whether individual CELLS within a population switch synchronously. The design operationalizes this via dispersion ACROSS INDEPENDENT SEEDS (separate simulator runs), which is a proxy for run-to-run stochastic variability, not within-population cell-to-cell heterogeneity. A simulator seed likely represents a single lineage trajectory per run, so high across-seed CV shows that replicate population-average trajectories differ from each other, which is a distinct claim from 'not all cells switch at the same time within one population.' The hypothesis should either justify why across-seed dispersion is a valid stand-in for within-population asynchrony, or reframe the claim/falsifier explicitly as being about population-average switch timing variability (not single-cell synchrony).

Rival B's discriminator relies on comparing dispersion/BC of growth_rate between wildtype and relA-knockout under the same shift — but growth_rate and ppgpp_conc are mechanistically coupled in the stringent response, so if relA knockout simply dampens ppGpp induction globally (shifting the mean), it could also mechanically reduce growth_rate variance for reasons other than 'turning off the asynchrony-generating mechanism' (e.g. simply flattening the whole dynamic range so there's less to be variable about). The design doesn't separate 'reduced dispersion because synchrony restored' from 'reduced dispersion because the whole response is suppressed/flattened.'

The relA-knockout control for Rival A assumes that if ribosome_conc decline is still synchronous (low CV) in the relA KO, this proves the underlying switch-sensing was synchronous all along. But relA KO removes the (p)ppGpp-dependent translational feedback pathway entirely, so ribosome_conc dynamics in that background could follow a qualitatively different (slower, ppGpp-independent) regulatory route unrelated to the wildtype switch mechanism. A tight distribution there would not necessarily show anything about the timing of the real stringent-response switch in wildtype cells; it only shows that a different control loop is deterministic.

The decision rule mixes 'Primary: BC>0.555' with a separate 'Secondary/confirmatory' welch test, but the falsifier/refuting_result section requires BOTH BC<=0.555 AND welch_t<2 to refute H1. This leaves an ambiguous middle zone (e.g., BC>0.555 but welch_t<2, or BC<=0.555 but welch_t>=2) where neither H1 nor H0 is clearly declared, weakening the risky prohibition.

The model's 'seeds' most likely instantiate independent whole-population (bulk) simulation runs with randomized initial/parameter draws, not individual cells within one shared population. The claim is about per-cell asynchrony WITHIN a population, but the operationalization pools across seeds (separate simulation replicates), which conflates population-replicate variance with single-cell heterogeneity.

hypothesis.question: How do bacteria choose between two sugars in the same flask?
hypothesis.claim: Diauxie / carbon catabolite repression constrains the model: since glucose uptake is modeled as a binary switch, the simulated 'choice' between two sugars collapses to glucose always winning via stringent-response-linked repression machinery, so an amino-acid downshift (the nearest in-envelope proxy for a nutrient-quality shift) will show the hallmark stringent-response signature (ppGpp spike, growth-rate drop) rather than any gradual blended uptake, while a relA knockout abolishes that signature — demonstrating that what looks like 'sugar choice' in this instrument is actually a ppGpp-gated growth-rate/resource-allocation response, not a dedicated sugar-preference circuit.
hypothesis.h1: An amino-acid downshift (minimal_plus_amino_acids -> minimal, proxy for the hierarchical-uptake decision) triggers a stringent-response-dependent growth arrest: ppgpp_conc rises >=3-fold and growth_rate falls >=40% relative to wildtype/basal within 2 generations, and this response is abolished (ppgpp_conc change <20%, growth_rate change <10%, both measured relative to the relA-KO's OWN basal baseline) when relA is knocked out, showing the 'choice' mechanism is ppGpp-mediated resource reallocation rather than a dedicated dual-sugar sensing circuit.
hypothesis.h0: ppgpp_conc and growth_rate in the amino_acid_shift/downshift design do not differ from wildtype/basal beyond replicate noise (|welch_t|<2), and/or the relA knockout shows the same magnitude of ppGpp/growth-rate change (relative to its own basal) as wildtype shows under the same shift (i.e. the response is not relA-dependent).

operational_defs.construct: nutritional downshift / hierarchical resource reallocation (proxy for sugar-choice switching)
operational_defs.observable: amino_acid_shift timeline event removing amino acids from media
operational_defs.measure: timeline design: '0 minimal_plus_amino_acids, 60 minimal' vs wildtype/basal control

operational_defs.observable: ppgpp_conc channel
operational_defs.measure: fold-change in mean ppgpp_conc post-shift vs wildtype/basal, averaged across seeds, at generation 2

operational_defs.construct: growth arrest / resource reallocation toward survival (mean-level)
operational_defs.observable: growth_rate channel
operational_defs.measure: % drop in mean growth_rate post-shift vs wildtype/basal, at generation 2

operational_defs.construct: causal dependence on RelA/SpoT pathway (relative-to-own-baseline, not absolute dispersion)
operational_defs.observable: rela_conc channel and ppgpp_conc channel in relA knockout background
operational_defs.measure: ppgpp_conc and growth_rate fold-change in gene_knockout(relA)+amino_acid_shift vs gene_knockout(relA)/basal (its OWN matched baseline, not wildtype/basal) — this isolates mean-shift abolition from any dispersion-flattening artifact

hypothesis.predicted_effect: Amino-acid downshift causes mean ppgpp_conc to rise >=3-fold (300%) and mean growth_rate to fall >=40% relative to wildtype/basal within 2 generations (Welch t vs reference, |t|>=2); in the relA-knockout background, the SAME shift applied relative to the relA-KO's OWN basal baseline shows both effects abolished (ppgpp_conc change <20%, growth_rate change <10%, |t|<2 vs relA-KO/basal) — i.e. an ~80-100% attenuation of the mean-level induction, not merely a narrowing of across-seed spread. This mean-vs-own-baseline comparison directly addresses objection r1.1/r1.2: it tests whether the INDUCTION itself is abolished (a causal claim about mechanism), not whether variance shrinks (which could be a flattening artifact or a different control loop).

falsifier.decision_rule: Welch t of ppgpp_conc, amino_acid_shift/downshift vs wildtype/basal across seeds at generation 2; reject H0 if two-sided |welch_t|>=2. Discriminating control: gene_knockout(relA)+amino_acid_shift/downshift must show |welch_t|<2 for ppgpp_conc AND growth_rate when compared against its OWN matched baseline gene_knockout(relA)/basal (NOT wildtype/basal) — this isolates whether the mean induction is abolished by loss of relA, rather than inferring mechanism from a change in dispersion/CV (which could reflect flattening rather than restored synchrony).
falsifier.refuting_result: ppgpp_conc in amino_acid_shift/downshift does not differ from wildtype/basal (|welch_t|<2), OR the relA knockout (vs its own basal) shows an equally large mean ppGpp/growth-rate shift as wildtype shows vs its basal (|welch_t|>=2 in the KO-vs-KO-basal comparison too), indicating the mean-level response is not RelA-dependent.

test.statistic: welch_t
test.threshold: |welch_t|>=2 for amino_acid_shift/downshift vs wildtype/basal; |welch_t|<2 for gene_knockout(relA)+amino_acid_shift/downshift vs gene_knockout(relA)/basal

rivals.claim: The growth-rate drop under amino-acid downshift is driven by generic amino-acid biosynthesis limitation (charged-tRNA depletion feeding translation directly), independent of ppGpp signaling per se — ppGpp is a correlated bystander, not causal.
rivals.distinguishing_result: If true, gene_knockout(relA)+amino_acid_shift/downshift vs its own basal would STILL show growth_rate change >=40% even though ppgpp_conc change stays <20%, because translation is limited directly by fraction_trna_charged regardless of RelA activity — i.e. the mean growth effect persists while the mean ppGpp effect is abolished, decoupling the two.

rivals.claim: The response is driven by ribosome-capacity reallocation (rRNA operon output) rather than ppGpp per se — cells slow growth because ribosome synthesis is throttled by a ppGpp-independent feedback loop.
rivals.distinguishing_result: rrna_operon_knockout/basal (no amino-acid shift) would show a similar mean growth_rate decline (>=40% vs wildtype/basal) even without any ppgpp_conc elevation (change <20%), showing ribosome capacity alone — not ppGpp signaling — can produce the phenotype, independent of the relA pathway.

auxiliary_assumptions: Glucose uptake is modeled as a binary switch (per instrument note), so a genuine two-sugar co-utilization/preference test is not directly expressible; amino_acid_shift is used as the best in-envelope proxy for a hierarchical nutrient-reallocation decision.

ppgpp_conc and rela_conc channels are only recorded under steady-state charging or when the kinetic RelA/SpoT module is explicitly on; this run assumes default steady-state charging mode where these channels are populated.
The relA gene_knockout is assumed to be mechanistically simulated (removes RelA synthetase activity) in this model build; this is checked downstream per the instrument note.

Seeds (isogenic replicates) capture intrinsic stochastic noise; deterministic vs stochastic origin of any residual variability is not adjudicated by this test and is treated as out of scope (per r1.3, flagged explicitly rather than chased further).

2 generations post-shift is assumed sufficient for the stringent response to manifest in ppgpp_conc and growth_rate, based on typical fast stringent-response kinetics (minutes-scale) relative to a generation (~hour-scale).

The relA-KO-vs-own-basal comparison (rather than relA-KO-vs-wildtype-basal) is used specifically to test mean-level induction abolition, sidestepping any dispersion/CV-based inference that could confound 'restored synchrony' with 'flattened dynamic range' (objections r1.1, r1.2); dispersion/bimodality claims about single-cell asynchrony are explicitly NOT made by this test and remain out of scope per r1.3.

objection_ledger.issue: Rival B's discriminator relies on comparing dispersion/BC of growth_rate between wildtype and relA-knockout under the same shift — but growth_rate and ppgpp_conc are mechanistically coupled in the stringent response, so if relA knockout simply dampens ppGpp induction globally (shifting the mean), it could also mechanically reduce growth_rate variance for reasons other than 'turning off the asynchrony-generating mechanism' (e.g. simply flattening the whole dynamic range so there's less to be variable about). The design doesn't separate 'reduced dispersion because synchrony restored' from 'reduced dispersion because the whole response is suppressed/flattened.'

The relA-knockout control for Rival A assumes that if ribosome_conc decline is still synchronous (low CV) in the relA KO, this proves the underlying switch-sensing was synchronous all along. But relA KO removes the (p)ppGpp-dependent translational feedback pathway entirely, so ribosome_conc dynamics in that background could follow a qualitatively different (slower, ppGpp-independent) regulatory route unrelated to the wildtype switch mechanism. A tight distribution there would not necessarily show anything about the timing of the real stringent-response switch in wildtype cells; it only shows that a different control loop is deterministic.

The instrument appears to be a population-level/few-seed stochastic simulator; 'cell-to-cell heterogeneity' and 'bimodality across isogenic cells' are being operationalized as variance across 8 independent simulation seeds, not actual single-cell measurements within one population. This is a real gap between the claim (within-population single-cell asynchrony) and what 8 seeds of a possibly deterministic-per-seed model can show, but the candidate already flags this as an explicit auxiliary assumption.

drafts.question: How do bacteria choose between two sugars in the same flask?
drafts.claim: E. coli's choice between two sugars is implemented as catabolite-repression-driven sequential use, and in this whole-cell model that mechanism is readable as a ppGpp/stringent-response-mediated growth-rate penalty when the preferred carbon source's uptake pathway is removed, forcing reliance on the alternative (lower-quality) substrate: knocking out the gene(s) needed for the preferred sugar's uptake (modeled here via a static media condition contrast, since the simulator does not support a true mixed-sugar switch) will drop growth rate and raise ppGpp relative to growth on the preferred substrate, mimicking the diauxic hierarchy.
drafts.h1: Loss of the preferred-sugar utilization gene (forcing metabolism onto the inferior static carbon condition) causes a substantial growth-rate decrease (>=25% drop) accompanied by a significant rise in ppgpp_conc (>=30% increase) relative to wildtype growth on the preferred (basal/glucose-like) condition, consistent with the stringent-response signature of a forced shift down the catabolite-repression hierarchy.
drafts.h0: Growth rate and ppgpp_conc on the inferior static carbon condition (with the uptake gene intact) do not differ significantly from wildtype on the preferred basal condition beyond replicate noise (|welch_t| < 2 for both channels).

operational_defs.observable: growth_rate
operational_defs.measure: instantaneous specific growth rate (1/h) under wildtype/basal condition

operational_defs.observable: growth_rate
operational_defs.measure: instantaneous specific growth rate (1/h) under wildtype/acetate condition (a static-only carbon source standing in for the lower-ranked sugar)

operational_defs.observable: ppgpp_conc
operational_defs.measure: steady-state ppGpp concentration (uM) averaged over the run

operational_defs.observable: growth_rate + division_rate
operational_defs.measure: growth rate and division fraction under a knockout of the preferred-sugar uptake gene run on basal condition (forcing flux through the inferior pathway machinery)

drafts.predicted_effect: Directional, multi-channel: growth_rate on acetate (or ptsG-knockout/basal) drops by ~25-40% relative to wildtype/basal (e.g. 0.9/h -> 0.55-0.65/h), while ppgpp_conc rises ~30-60% (e.g. 20uM -> 28-32uM), reflecting the stringent-response signature of a forced downshift in the catabolite hierarchy; division_rate may also drop modestly (<10%) if the KO is not lethal.

falsifier.decision_rule: Welch t of ppgpp_conc, ptsG-knockout/basal vs wildtype/basal, across seeds; reject H0 if |welch_t|>=2 (two-sided) AND effect_pct indicates >=30% increase in the KO
falsifier.refuting_result: ppgpp_conc in ptsG-knockout/basal is statistically indistinguishable from wildtype/basal (|welch_t|<2) or shows <10% change, showing the forced pathway loss does NOT trigger a stringent-response-scale signal, undermining the catabolite-repression/stringent-response link

test.statistic: welch_t
test.threshold: |t|>=2 and effect_pct>=30%

rivals.claim: The growth/ppGpp change is simply a generic nutrient-quality effect of acetate vs glucose media (static condition difference), not a gene-choice/catabolite-repression-specific mechanism -- i.e. ANY static media of lower quality gives the same signature regardless of whether a specific uptake gene is knocked out.
rivals.distinguishing_result: If wildtype/acetate (no KO) shows the same ppGpp rise and growth drop magnitude as ptsG-knockout/basal, the effect is attributable to generic media quality, not to loss of the specific preferred-sugar uptake machinery.

rivals.claim: The ppGpp rise is not causally required for the growth-rate drop (growth rate drop is driven purely by metabolic/FBA flux limitation, not by a stringent-response regulatory loop) -- i.e. ppGpp is an epiphenomenal co-mover rather than a driver.
rivals.distinguishing_result: In a relA-knockout background (abolishing ppGpp synthesis capacity) combined with the same preferred-sugar uptake loss, if growth_rate still drops by a similar magnitude as in the ppGpp-intact KO, this shows the growth defect is independent of the stringent response, refuting the mechanistic coupling implied by H1.

auxiliary_assumptions: Deleting ptsG is an adequate proxy for 'losing access to the preferred sugar' in this model, since the simulator does not support a true two-sugar mixed-media switch.
Static acetate condition is an adequate stand-in for a generically inferior static carbon source enabling a media-quality control comparison.

A combined relA+ptsG double knockout is within the envelope as a single multi_gene_knockout-style perturbation (not a forbidden ppgpp_conc+gene_knockout combination) and serves as the interventional control isolating ppGpp-dependence.
Steady-state charging mode is used (ppgpp_conc and ribosome_conc are valid channels under this mode); kinetic ppGpp module is not invoked.
Per-seed stochastic noise at 6 seeds / 3 generations is sufficient to detect a >=30% effect size via Welch's t at the stated threshold (not separately power-checked here).

drafts.question: How do bacteria choose between two sugars in the same flask?
drafts.claim: Carbon catabolite repression via the stringent/ppGpp-coupled regulatory axis causes E. coli to prioritize one sugar over a second, alternative carbon source by suppressing growth-rate contribution and shifting physiology toward a single-substrate-like state even when a second sugar is nominally available — i.e., the simulated 'choice' manifests as the mixed condition behaving statistically like the preferred-sugar-only condition rather than an intermediate/blended state. Since this simulator exposes only static fitted media conditions (no true simultaneous two-sugar mixed condition), we operationalize 'choice between two sugars' as comparing a glucose-only basal condition against an alternative static carbon condition (acetate) and testing whether physiological state under acetate shows hallmarks of catabolite-repression-like deprioritization (elevated ppGpp, reduced growth rate, reduced ribosome concentration) relative to glucose — consistent with glucose being the preferred/chosen substrate when both would be present.
drafts.h1: Growth rate, ribosome concentration, and ppGpp concentration under the non-preferred static carbon condition (acetate) differ from glucose/basal in the direction predicted by a hierarchical-preference (catabolite repression) model: acetate condition shows lower growth_rate (>=40% reduction), lower ribosome_conc (>=25% reduction), and higher ppgpp_conc (>=50% increase) relative to basal, reflecting that cells deprioritize the poorer substrate in a manner consistent with a chosen hierarchy rather than symmetric substrate use.
drafts.h0: There is no systematic difference in growth_rate, ribosome_conc, or ppgpp_conc between basal (glucose) and acetate conditions beyond replicate noise — i.e., the simulator's static media-fitting treats alternative carbon sources as physiologically interchangeable rather than reflecting a preference hierarchy.

operational_defs.observable: ppgpp_conc
operational_defs.measure: mean ppgpp_conc (uM) per seed, basal vs acetate, Welch t-test across seeds

operational_defs.observable: growth_rate
operational_defs.measure: mean instantaneous growth_rate (1/h) per seed, basal vs acetate

operational_defs.observable: ribosome_conc
operational_defs.measure: mean ribosome_conc (uM) per seed, basal vs acetate
