operational_defs.measure: mean growth_rate (1/h) across seeds under basal condition, pre-shift window

operational_defs.observable: growth_rate
operational_defs.measure: % reduction in steady-state growth_rate of ppgpp_conc-clamped design vs wildtype/basal across seeds

operational_defs.observable: growth_rate and fraction_trna_charged trajectories after amino_acid_shift removal event
operational_defs.measure: mean growth_rate and fraction_trna_charged during the 60-120 min window post-shift, compared target vs reference

drafts.predicted_effect: Pre-shift: ppgpp_conc=2x clamp reduces mean growth_rate by ~15-25% vs wildtype/basal (fold-change ~0.75-0.85). Post-shift (amino acid removal): wildtype growth_rate drops sharply (>50% reduction) and fraction_trna_charged crashes, while the primed (ppgpp clamp) strain shows a smaller relative post-shift growth_rate drop (<25% reduction) and higher post-shift fraction_trna_charged (target ~1.3-1.5x reference), producing a crossover where integrated growth over the full timeline favors the primed strain once the shift occurs.

falsifier.decision_rule: Welch t-test of growth_rate, ppgpp_conc-clamped target vs wildtype reference, computed separately for the pre-shift window and the post-shift (amino_acid_shift) window across seeds; reject H0 for the pre-shift cost if |t|>=2 with target mean lower; reject H0 for the recovery-benefit claim if |t|>=2 with target mean HIGHER than reference in the post-shift window (i.e., the sign of the effect must flip between windows)
falsifier.refuting_result: No pre-shift growth deficit (|t|<2) OR no post-shift relative advantage (|t|<2, or target still lower than reference post-shift) — i.e., the clamp is a pure cost with no compensating benefit, disconfirming the bet-hedging crossover

test.statistic: welch_t
test.threshold: |t|>=2 pre-shift (target<reference) AND |t|>=2 post-shift (target>reference)

rivals.claim: Rival A: ppGpp elevation is simply growth-rate-limiting with no conditional benefit (pure cost, no bet-hedging) — the stringent response only matters AFTER a shift is already underway via feedback, not as a pre-emptive strategy.
rivals.distinguishing_result: If true, the relA knockout control (which abolishes ppGpp induction during the shift) would show WORSE post-shift recovery than wildtype (confirming ppGpp's reactive role) while the pre-clamped primed strain shows NO additional benefit over wildtype post-shift — i.e., priming in advance adds nothing beyond what the normal reactive stringent response already provides.

rivals.claim: Rival B: any apparent post-shift advantage in the ppGpp-clamped strain is an artifact of a lower pre-shift ribosome/growth baseline (less far to fall), not a genuine preparedness mechanism tied to charged-tRNA buffering.
rivals.distinguishing_result: If true, fraction_trna_charged trajectories would be similar between target and reference post-shift (no buffering difference) even though growth_rate differs, showing the growth-rate effect is decoupled from the proposed tRNA-charging mechanism.

auxiliary_assumptions: The ppgpp_conc clamp at 2x basal is a valid proxy for a naturally occurring 'primed' subpopulation phenotype, even though the simulator does not generate spontaneous bet-hedging heterogeneity itself.
amino_acid_shift removal mid-run is a sufficiently sharp perturbation to distinguish prepared vs unprepared physiology within 1-4 generations.
Growth_rate and fraction_trna_charged measured at steady-state charging are comparable across the clamp and relA-knockout designs (both run under steady-state charging mode, not kinetic).

Seed-to-seed stochastic variation is the dominant noise source we are controlling for via Welch's t across 4-8 seeds; deterministic-vs-stochastic ambiguity in single-seed trajectories is out of scope for this test.

drafts.question: Can it ever help a population for some cells to grow slowly or stay 'prepared' for a change?
drafts.claim: A bet-hedging subpopulation that maintains elevated stringent-response "preparedness" (higher basal ppGpp and RelA, slower growth) at steady state incurs a fitness cost in constant rich/basal media but this is the same mechanism that confers a survival/adaptation advantage upon a sudden nutritional downshift — i.e., preparedness is a population-level insurance strategy, not individually optimal in a static environment.
drafts.h1: Across isogenic seeds, cells/lineages with elevated basal ppgpp_conc and rela_conc (and correspondingly lower growth_rate) in constant basal medium show a smaller growth-rate COLLAPSE (smaller relative drop in growth_rate and smaller drop in division_rate) upon an amino-acid downshift than low-ppGpp lineages, despite paying a steady-state growth penalty of ~10-20% in the unperturbed condition.
drafts.h0: Basal ppgpp_conc/rela_conc level does not predict differential resilience to the downshift: growth_rate and division_rate drop by the same relative amount in the shift timeline regardless of pre-shift ppGpp/RelA level, and any steady-state growth difference between high- and low-ppGpp conditions is noise-level (<5%, welch_t<2).

operational_defs.observable: ppgpp_conc and rela_conc
operational_defs.measure: mean ppgpp_conc (uM) and rela_conc (uM) over the pre-shift window, compared between a ppgpp_conc-clamped-high design and wildtype/basal

operational_defs.observable: growth_rate
operational_defs.measure: % difference in mean growth_rate between ppgpp_conc-clamped-high/basal and wildtype/basal across seeds

operational_defs.observable: growth_rate and division_rate
operational_defs.measure: relative drop (%) in growth_rate and division_rate from pre-shift baseline to post-shift trough, compared between high-ppGpp and wildtype timelines

drafts.predicted_effect: Steady state: ppgpp_conc-clamped-high/basal shows growth_rate ~10-20% lower than wildtype/basal (Welch |t|>=2). Downshift: wildtype/timeline shows a growth_rate drop of ~40-60% and division_rate drop of ~30-50% at the post-shift trough, whereas ppgpp_conc-clamped-high/timeline shows a substantially smaller relative drop (~15-25% in growth_rate, ~10-20% in division_rate) — i.e. roughly half the relative collapse magnitude.

falsifier.decision_rule: Welch t of relative growth_rate drop (pre-shift mean minus post-shift trough mean, as % of pre-shift mean) between ppgpp_conc-clamped-high/timeline and wildtype/timeline across seeds; reject H0 if |t|>=2 AND the high-ppGpp relative drop is smaller (less negative) than wildtype's
falsifier.refuting_result: the relative growth_rate drop in ppgpp_conc-clamped-high/timeline is statistically indistinguishable from wildtype/timeline (|t|<2) or is equal/larger, showing no resilience benefit from elevated basal ppGpp

test.statistic: welch_t

rivals.claim: High basal ppGpp is simply a slow-growth phenotype with no special shift-resilience; any apparent protection is just that slower-growing cells have a smaller absolute distance to fall (a ceiling/floor artifact of growth_rate scale), not an adaptive insurance mechanism.
rivals.distinguishing_result: If true, the RELATIVE (percentage) drop in growth_rate would be the SAME between high-ppGpp and wildtype once normalized to pre-shift baseline (no significant difference in % drop, |t|<2), even though absolute drop differs.

rivals.claim: RelA/SpoT-driven ppGpp induction DURING the shift (not pre-existing basal level) is what confers resilience; basal/clamped ppGpp before the shift is irrelevant, and a relA knockout (which abolishes the ability to induce ppGpp at the shift) should show the real protective effect, not the pre-shift clamp.
rivals.distinguishing_result: If true, a relA gene_knockout/timeline design would show a LARGER collapse (bigger relative drop) than wildtype/timeline despite having normal or even elevated basal ppGpp from the clamp control, because it cannot mount the dynamic ppGpp spike at the shift moment.

auxiliary_assumptions: The ppgpp_conc clamp at 2.5x basal is a reasonable proxy for a naturally-occurring high-preparedness subpopulation/phenotypic state, even though it is an exogenous clamp rather than an emergent bimodal distribution.

The amino-acid downshift timeline (removing amino acids at t=1200) is a valid operationalization of a 'sudden nutritional change' that stresses the translation/charging system enough to perturb growth_rate and division_rate measurably within 4 generations.
Steady-state charging mode is used (not kinetic) so ppgpp_conc, rela_conc, and ribosome_conc channels are all available and directly comparable across designs.
Division_rate and growth_rate respond on a timescale compatible with 4 simulated generations; if the trough has not resolved by generation 4, the effect may be underestimated rather than absent.
Seeds (n=6) are assumed to give adequate replicate power for the Welch comparison; this is not a formal power calculation but a pragmatic modest-scale choice per platform guidance.

drafts.question: Can it ever help a population for some cells to grow slowly or stay 'prepared' for a change?
drafts.claim: Bet-hedging via stringent-response priming is adaptive at the population level: a subpopulation of cells that constitutively hold elevated ppGpp (and thus grow slower, with lower ribosome concentration) under steady nutrient-rich conditions will show a growth-rate advantage over an unprimed (ppGpp-clamped-low) population specifically when challenged by an abrupt nutrient downshift, even though the primed population grows slower under the stable condition itself.
drafts.h1: Across seeds, a ppGpp-elevated ('primed') population has lower mean growth_rate than wildtype under stable basal media (cost of preparedness), but shows a smaller growth_rate drop (and faster division_rate recovery) than wildtype immediately after an amino-acid downshift timeline event (benefit of preparedness) — i.e. the rank order of population mean growth_rate between primed and wildtype REVERSES between the stable and shift conditions.
drafts.h0: Priming (elevated ppGpp_conc clamp) confers no growth_rate or division_rate benefit after the downshift relative to wildtype; the primed population is simply uniformly slower-growing in both the stable and shift conditions (no rank reversal), i.e. growth_rate(primed) <= growth_rate(wildtype) in both conditions with no significant differential response.

operational_defs.observable: ppgpp_conc clamped to an elevated multiple of basal
operational_defs.measure: ppgpp_conc channel value, set via the ppgpp_conc perturbation to e.g. 2x basal

operational_defs.construct: cost of preparedness under stable growth
operational_defs.observable: growth_rate under basal condition, no shift
operational_defs.measure: mean growth_rate across seeds/generations in wildtype/basal vs ppgpp_conc(2x)/basal

operational_defs.construct: benefit of preparedness after nutrient downshift
operational_defs.observable: growth_rate and division_rate immediately following an amino-acid-withdrawal timeline event
operational_defs.measure: mean growth_rate and division_rate in the post-shift window across seeds, compared between primed and wildtype

drafts.predicted_effect: Rank reversal with two components: (1) under stable basal, primed population growth_rate is ~15-25% lower than wildtype (e.g. 1.2/h vs 1.5/h, Cohen's-d-scale fold-change ~0.8x); (2) after amino-acid downshift, primed population growth_rate drop is attenuated — wildtype growth_rate falls by ~50% from pre-shift baseline while primed falls by only ~15-20%, and primed division_rate stays >=0.9 while wildtype division_rate drops below 0.7, a differential-response effect size (Welch t on the shift-vs-stable delta) with |t|>=2.

falsifier.decision_rule: Welch t-test on growth_rate measured in the post-downshift window, primed (ppgpp_conc clamp) vs wildtype, both under the amino_acid_shift timeline, across seeds; reject H0 if |t|>=2 AND effect direction shows primed > wildtype post-shift growth_rate (i.e. primed loses less). Paired with the stable-condition Welch t (ppgpp_conc/basal vs wildtype/basal) confirming primed < wildtype there, to establish the reversal.
falsifier.refuting_result: Welch |t|<2 on the post-shift growth_rate comparison, or primed growth_rate is NOT greater than wildtype post-shift (no attenuation of the downshift penalty), indicating priming confers no shift-specific benefit and is simply a uniform cost — no rank reversal.

test.statistic: welch_t
test.threshold: |t|>=2, with sign requiring primed>wildtype growth_rate post-shift

rivals.claim: Ribosome-capacity limitation (not ppGpp signaling per se) explains any apparent benefit: simply having fewer ribosomes (rrna_operon_knockout) at steady state, independent of ppGpp, would show the same attenuated downshift penalty, meaning the effect is about ribosome stoichiometry, not stringent-response regulation.
rivals.distinguishing_result: If rrna_operon_knockout/basal_shift shows the SAME attenuated growth_rate drop post-shift as ppgpp_conc(2x)/basal_shift, the benefit is attributable to constitutive ribosome limitation rather than ppGpp-mediated regulatory flexibility, undermining the ppGpp-specific priming claim.

rivals.claim: The apparent benefit is an artifact of regression to the mean / survivorship: primed cells are already near a floor growth rate, so any perturbation looks smaller in relative terms purely due to compressed dynamic range, not genuine preparedness.
rivals.distinguishing_result: If the ABSOLUTE (not relative) growth_rate drop (delta, not fold-change) is statistically indistinguishable between primed and wildtype (Welch t on absolute deltas |t|<2), the apparent 'attenuation' is a scaling artifact rather than a true physiological buffering effect.

auxiliary_assumptions: The ppgpp_conc clamp perturbation mechanistically suppresses ribosome synthesis/activity in the simulator similarly to the native stringent response (i.e. the clamp is not purely cosmetic on the ppgpp_conc channel but propagates to ribosome_conc and growth_rate).
The amino_acid_shift timeline event (withdrawal) is simulated as a genuine nutrient downshift that stresses translation capacity, not merely a bookkeeping label change.

Population-level 'benefit' is operationalized as the AVERAGE behavior across isogenic seeds under a single shared perturbation (clamped ppGpp), not as true within-population heterogeneity/bet-hedging with two coexisting subtypes in one run, since the instrument applies one perturbation per design; this is a scope caveat — we test the regulatory-strategy's population consequence via between-design comparison rather than a mixed-subpopulation competition experiment.
Division_rate and growth_rate are read in a comparable post-shift window across designs (same generation index) so that transient dynamics are aligned.

select_score.question: Can it ever help a population for some cells to grow slowly or stay 'prepared' for a change?
select_score.claim: Bet-hedging via stringent-response 'preparedness': a subpopulation of isogenic E. coli cells that maintain elevated ppGpp and slower growth even in nutrient-replete (basal) conditions will show a growth-rate advantage over the bulk population specifically when challenged by a sudden nutrient downshift (amino-acid withdrawal), because their pre-activated stringent response buffers the shock. In steady favorable conditions this preparedness is a fitness cost (lower mean growth rate / bimodal growth-rate distribution), but it becomes a population-level benefit under fluctuating/shift conditions (faster recovery, less growth-rate collapse) relative to a population lacking this heterogeneity (e.g., a relA knockout that cannot mount ppGpp pre-induction).
select_score.h1: In basal (favorable, steady) conditions, isogenic wildtype populations exhibit a bimodal/heterogeneous ppGpp and growth-rate distribution (slow-growing, high-ppGpp subpopulation present), and upon an amino-acid downshift timeline, wildtype populations show a significantly smaller growth-rate drop (less collapse / faster recovery) than a relA-knockout population that lacks stringent-response heterogeneity.
select_score.h0: ppGpp/growth-rate heterogeneity in basal conditions is unimodal (no distinct 'prepared' subpopulation; bimodality_bc <= 0.555), AND/OR the relA-knockout population shows no significant difference in growth-rate drop upon amino-acid downshift compared to wildtype (|welch_t| < 2 on growth_rate effect_pct between wildtype/downshift and relA_knockout/downshift).

operational_defs.construct: growth cost of preparedness in steady state
operational_defs.observable: growth_rate
operational_defs.measure: mean growth_rate and its distribution shape (bimodality_bc) across seeds in basal condition, wildtype vs relA_knockout

operational_defs.observable: growth_rate
operational_defs.measure: percent drop in growth_rate (effect_pct) immediately after amino_acid downshift timeline event, compared between wildtype and relA_knockout

operational_defs.construct: bet-hedging mechanism specificity (not just slower baseline growth)
operational_defs.observable: fraction_trna_charged
operational_defs.measure: trajectory of fraction_trna_charged post-shift, wildtype vs relA_knockout, as a mechanistic correlate of the stringent response buffering charged-tRNA depletion

select_score.predicted_effect: (1) In basal/wildtype, ppgpp_conc and growth_rate pooled across seeds show a bimodal distribution with Sarle's BC > 0.6, consistent with ~10-20% of trajectories/seeds in a 'high-ppGpp, slow-growth' (prepared) regime (growth_rate roughly 30-50% lower than the fast mode). (2) Upon amino_acid_shift downshift, wildtype growth_rate drops by only ~15-25% (effect_pct) relative to its own pre-shift baseline, whereas relA_knockout growth_rate drops by ~40-60%, i.e. a >=2-fold larger collapse in the knockout, with Welch |t|>=2 between wildtype/downshift and relA_knockout/downshift on growth_rate.

falsifier.decision_rule: Welch t of growth_rate effect_pct (post-shift drop relative to pre-shift baseline), relA_knockout/downshift vs wildtype/downshift across seeds; reject H0 (no protective benefit of preparedness) if |welch_t| >= 2 with relA_knockout showing a LARGER drop (more negative effect_pct) than wildtype
falsifier.refuting_result: relA_knockout/downshift shows growth_rate drop statistically indistinguishable from wildtype/downshift (|welch_t| < 2), or relA_knockout actually recovers BETTER than wildtype, indicating stringent-response heterogeneity confers no protective population benefit

test.statistic: welch_t
test.threshold: |t| >= 2, with sign indicating relA_knockout drop > wildtype drop

rivals.claim: Rival A: observed growth-rate/ppGpp heterogeneity in basal conditions is just intrinsic stochastic noise in ribosome/metabolic flux allocation, unrelated to any adaptive 'preparedness' function, and relA deletion simply removes a constitutive growth-rate brake (uniformly slower baseline) rather than removing a bet-hedging subpopulation.
rivals.distinguishing_result: If true, basal ppgpp_conc/growth_rate distributions in wildtype would be UNIMODAL (bimodality_bc <= 0.555) rather than bimodal, and relA_knockout would show a uniformly shifted (not differentially protected) growth_rate trajectory post-shift — i.e. relA_knockout baseline growth_rate would be faster than wildtype in basal AND show the SAME proportional drop on downshift.

rivals.claim: Rival B: any apparent protection in wildtype after downshift is driven purely by generic ribosome-capacity reserve (more ribosomes per cell), not by ppGpp/stringent-response signaling per se — i.e. it's a ribosome_conc effect, not a regulatory bet-hedging effect.
rivals.distinguishing_result: An rrna_operon_knockout/downshift control (reduced ribosome capacity but intact ppGpp signaling) would show a growth_rate drop similar to wildtype (ppGpp-mediated buffering still works despite lower ribosome reserve), whereas if Rival B were true, rrna_operon_knockout would show a drop as large as relA_knockout, implicating ribosome capacity rather than ppGpp signaling as the protective factor.

auxiliary_assumptions: The simulator's stochastic seed-to-seed variation in basal condition approximates genuine isogenic cell-to-cell heterogeneity (bet-hedging subpopulations), even though each run is a single-lineage trajectory rather than an explicit multi-cell population snapshot; bimodality is assessed over pooled per-seed per-timepoint values as a proxy for population heterogeneity.

relA knockout is assumed to be mechanistically simulated (abolishing (p)ppGpp synthesis induction) in this model version; if relA KO shows no ppgpp_conc change at all vs wildtype, this would indicate the knockout is not mechanistically implemented and the test is uninformative (a scope caveat, not evidence against H1).
The amino_acid_shift timeline event (minimal minus amino acids) is assumed to be a sufficient proxy for a 'sudden nutrient downshift' stress relevant to stringent-response activation.

Growth-rate effect_pct is computed relative to each condition's own pre-shift baseline (within-seed normalization) so that comparisons across wildtype and relA_knockout are not confounded by baseline growth-rate differences alone.

hypothesis.h0: ppGpp-clamped ('prepared') populations show no difference, or a strictly worse outcome, in growth_rate/division_rate resilience during and after the amino-acid downshift relative to wildtype; any baseline growth reduction is a pure cost with no compensating benefit under the shift.

division_rate under the amino-acid downshift timeline is assumed to be a valid proxy for population-level robustness/survival benefit of preparedness; we are not measuring long-run competitive fitness directly.

Basal condition is stable/rich enough that growth is fast for most cells, making a slow-growing high-ppGpp subpopulation costly in the short run — consistent with a bet-hedging (not mean-maximizing) interpretation.

drafts.question: Can it ever help a population for some cells to grow slowly or stay 'prepared' for a change?
drafts.claim: Bet-hedging via stringent-response priming: a subpopulation of cells that constitutively maintain elevated ppGpp (and thus slower growth, lower ribosome content) pays an individual fitness cost in steady nutrient-rich conditions but confers population-level resilience when an abrupt nutrient downshift occurs, because 'primed' cells avoid the growth-rate/division collapse that unprimed (low basal ppGpp) cells suffer during the shift.
drafts.h1: Across an amino-acid downshift timeline, cells/seeds with clamped elevated basal ppGpp (ppgpp_conc ~2-3x basal) show a smaller drop in growth_rate and higher division_rate immediately post-shift than wildtype cells with normal (lower, unclamped) basal ppGpp, despite having lower pre-shift growth_rate (a 15-30% growth penalty in steady state).
drafts.h0: Pre-primed (elevated basal ppGpp) cells show no difference in post-shift growth_rate or division_rate recovery compared to wildtype cells; any pre-shift growth penalty from elevated ppGpp is a pure cost with no compensating benefit during the shift (i.e., ppgpp_conc clamp does not causally buffer the shift response).

operational_defs.observable: ppgpp_conc
operational_defs.measure: steady-state ppgpp_conc level relative to wildtype basal, clamped via ppgpp_conc perturbation to 2-3x basal

operational_defs.observable: growth_rate
operational_defs.measure: mean growth_rate over pre-shift generations (0-1200 min) in primed vs wildtype, expressed as % reduction

operational_defs.observable: growth_rate, division_rate
operational_defs.measure: growth_rate trajectory and division_rate in the 1-2 generations immediately following the amino-acid downshift event (removal of amino acids at timeline switch)

operational_defs.observable: division_rate
operational_defs.measure: fraction of generations that successfully divide post-shift, compared between primed and wildtype across seeds

drafts.predicted_effect: Pre-shift: primed cells (ppgpp_conc clamp 2-3x) show 15-30% lower growth_rate than wildtype (steady-state cost). Post-shift (within 1-2 generations after amino acid removal): wildtype growth_rate drops by an additional 40-60% relative to its own pre-shift value, while primed cells drop by only 10-20% from their (already lower) pre-shift value — i.e., a crossover where primed cells' post-shift growth_rate exceeds wildtype's post-shift growth_rate by ~20-40%, and primed division_rate stays >=0.8 while wildtype division_rate falls below 0.6.

falsifier.decision_rule: Welch t-test of post-shift growth_rate (generations 2-3, after the amino-acid-removal timeline event) between ppgpp_conc-clamped and wildtype designs across seeds; reject H0 (i.e., support priming benefit) if |welch_t|>=2 AND the sign shows primed > wildtype post-shift growth_rate. Also require division_rate difference in the same direction (primed >= wildtype) as a corroborating check.
falsifier.refuting_result: Welch t |t|<2, or t>=2 but with wildtype post-shift growth_rate >= primed (i.e., no crossover, priming is a pure cost with no post-shift compensation), or division_rate shows no corroborating advantage for primed cells.

test.statistic: welch_t
test.threshold: |t|>=2 with sign primed>wildtype post-shift growth_rate

rivals.claim: Rival A: ppGpp elevation is purely a growth-rate brake with no anticipatory/preparedness function — the post-shift advantage (if any) is just because primed cells are already growing slowly, so they have 'less far to fall', not because they are biochemically prepared via pre-charged machinery or altered proteome allocation.
rivals.distinguishing_result: If true, a growth_rate-matched control (e.g., a different perturbation like rrna_operon_knockout that slows growth via reduced ribosome capacity WITHOUT elevating ppGpp) would show the SAME post-shift resilience as the ppGpp-clamped cells, since the benefit is just from having a lower pre-shift rate, not from ppGpp-specific stringent-response machinery.

rivals.claim: Rival B: the relA-dependent stringent response (natural ppGpp synthesis upon amino-acid starvation) is sufficient on its own for wildtype cells to cope with the downshift, so an artificial ppgpp_conc clamp confers no additional benefit beyond what endogenous RelA induction already provides; the clamp just imposes a constitutive cost with no added resilience.
rivals.distinguishing_result: A relA gene_knockout under amino_acid_downshift would show a MUCH WORSE post-shift growth_rate/division_rate crash than wildtype (since relA-KO cannot mount the natural stringent response), demonstrating the natural response matters; but if the ppgpp_conc-clamped primed cells perform no better than wildtype (only relA-KO is worse), that supports Rival B over H1.

auxiliary_assumptions: The simulator's amino_acid_shift / timeline mechanism for removing amino acids mid-run produces a genuine nutrient downshift stress detectable in growth_rate and fraction_trna_charged within 1-2 generations.
ppgpp_conc clamp at 2-3x basal is within the physiologically modeled range and does not itself cause division arrest or lethality (division_rate ~0) that would confound comparison.
Steady-state charging mode is used (not kinetic), so ppgpp_conc and ribosome_conc channels are valid readouts throughout.
Seeds (isogenic stochastic replicates) adequately sample intrinsic noise; 6 seeds give sufficient power for a Welch t at the predicted effect sizes (20-40% post-shift growth_rate difference).

The relA knockout and rrna_operon_knockout controls isolate mechanism without introducing confounded basal physiology beyond what the model already captures; residual confounds (e.g., pleiotropic effects of rRNA operon loss) are acknowledged as a scope caveat not fully resolvable in this simulator.

drafts.question: Can it ever help a population for some cells to grow slowly or stay 'prepared' for a change?
drafts.claim: A bet-hedging subpopulation that stays slow-growing / stress-prepared (high ppGpp, elevated RelA, lower growth rate) persists at a substantial, non-trivial frequency across isogenic replicates under steady favorable conditions, and this 'prepared' phenotype confers a growth-rate advantage specifically after an abrupt nutritional downshift — i.e. bimodality in growth_rate/ppgpp_conc is maintained even though it costs mean fitness in constant basal medium, consistent with a bet-hedging strategy rather than a uniform optimal growth rate.
drafts.h1: Across isogenic seeds under constant favorable (basal) conditions, the population shows a bimodal/heavy-tailed distribution of growth_rate and ppgpp_conc (a persistent slow/high-ppGpp subpopulation at roughly 10-30% frequency), and this subpopulation's prior higher ppGpp confers a growth-rate advantage (positive recovery slope) upon an amino-acid downshift, such that mean post-shift growth_rate is higher than in a matched population lacking this heterogeneity (relA knockout).
drafts.h0: Growth_rate and ppgpp_conc are unimodally distributed across seeds in constant basal medium (no persistent prepared subpopulation), and post-downshift growth recovery does not differ between wildtype and relA-knockout backgrounds (ppGpp-mediated preparedness confers no benefit) — i.e. any apparent slow-growth variance is just replicate/intrinsic noise with no distributional structure and no differential shift-survival benefit.

operational_defs.observable: growth_rate and ppgpp_conc per-seed distributions in wildtype/basal
operational_defs.measure: Sarle's bimodality coefficient (BC) over pooled per-seed growth_rate values; BC>0.555 flags bimodality; fraction in low-growth cluster from the best 2-cluster split

operational_defs.observable: ppgpp_conc, rela_conc channels
operational_defs.measure: per-seed mean ppgpp_conc and rela_conc; correlation with growth_rate cluster membership

operational_defs.construct: fitness benefit of preparedness after downshift
operational_defs.observable: growth_rate trajectory after an amino_acid_shift (removal) timeline event
operational_defs.measure: slope of growth_rate over the 2 generations following the shift, compared between wildtype (heterogeneous) and relA-knockout (homogeneous, low ppGpp) backgrounds via Welch t-test

drafts.predicted_effect: (1) In wildtype/basal, growth_rate distribution across seeds+timepoints is bimodal: BC > 0.555, with ~15-25% of mass in a low-growth (slow/prepared) cluster whose mean ppgpp_conc is >=2-fold the fast cluster's. (2) Following an amino-acid downshift, wildtype mean post-shift growth_rate recovery slope is higher than relA-knockout's by at least 30-50% (effect size ~0.3-0.5 in 1/h per generation), i.e. wildtype retains a higher post-shift growth_rate (~15-25% higher at 2 generations post-shift) despite a lower pre-shift population mean growth_rate (a cost of ~5-10%), consistent with a bet-hedging tradeoff.

falsifier.decision_rule: Welch t-test of post-shift growth_rate (generations 2-3 post amino-acid-removal shift) across seeds, wildtype (amino_acid_shift/basal_to_no_aa) vs relA-knockout (gene_knockout/basal_to_no_aa_relA); reject H0 (no preparedness benefit) if |welch_t| >= 2 with wildtype mean higher. Additionally, bimodality_bc on pooled wildtype/basal growth_rate values must exceed 0.555 to establish the prepared subpopulation exists at baseline.
falsifier.refuting_result: welch_t < 2 (or wildtype post-shift growth_rate mean is NOT higher than relA-KO), OR bimodality_bc <= 0.555 in wildtype/basal baseline (unimodal growth_rate distribution, no detectable prepared subpopulation) -- either result refutes H1.

test.statistic: welch_t
test.threshold: |t|>=2, wildtype mean higher than relA-KO

rivals.claim: Any observed growth_rate/ppgpp_conc variance is pure intrinsic stochastic noise with no adaptive distributional structure or functional consequence (noise-is-just-noise null).
rivals.distinguishing_result: bimodality_bc stays <=0.555 in wildtype/basal across seeds (unimodal, noisy-but-not-structured), and relA-KO shows statistically indistinguishable post-shift recovery from wildtype.

rivals.claim: Post-shift growth advantage in wildtype is NOT due to ppGpp-mediated preparedness but to generic higher baseline ribosome/protein reserves (a passive resource-storage effect unrelated to the stringent response).
rivals.distinguishing_result: relA-knockout (which abolishes ppGpp synthesis but leaves ribosome/protein mass largely intact) still recovers as fast as wildtype post-shift, showing the advantage tracks ribosome_conc/protein_mass rather than ppgpp_conc/rela_conc.

rivals.claim: The slow/prepared subpopulation is an artifact of simulation initialization transients (seed-to-seed variation in starting state) rather than a maintained steady-state bimodality.
rivals.distinguishing_result: bimodality_bc computed only on later generations (post generation 2, after transients settle) drops below 0.555, indicating the bimodality was a startup artifact, not a maintained population structure.

auxiliary_assumptions: The simulator's intrinsic noise model (seed-to-seed stochasticity in gene expression/charging) is the relevant source of heterogeneity for bet-hedging, not an artifact to be filtered out.

relA knockout is an adequate interventional control for 'no ppGpp-mediated stringent response capability' without also perturbing unrelated pathways (SpoT-mediated basal ppGpp synthesis/hydrolysis still operates and is treated as background).
An amino-acid-removal timeline event is a valid proxy for a naturally occurring nutritional downshift that would select for pre-adapted/prepared cells.

Growth_rate and ppgpp_conc measured at the population (per-seed, per-generation) level adequately approximate single-cell subpopulation structure given the instrument does not provide single-cell trajectories within a seed.

Division_rate is not confounded (i.e., the slow-growth cluster is not simply dying/non-dividing cells, which would be a distinct phenomenon from adaptive preparedness) -- this will be checked as a secondary read but is assumed resolvable by the main growth_rate/ppgpp bimodality + recovery test.

select_score.question: Can it ever help a population for some cells to grow slowly or stay 'prepared' for a change?
select_score.claim: A bet-hedging subpopulation that grows slowly with elevated ppGpp (a 'prepared'/persister-like state) is maintained even in constant favorable conditions, and this heterogeneity is adaptive: when challenged by an abrupt nutritional downshift, lineages/seeds that carry a higher fraction of slow-growing, high-ppGpp cells show a smaller collapse in growth rate and faster recovery than lineages without that reserve.
select_score.h1: Across an isogenic seed population under constant basal media, growth_rate and ppgpp_conc are bimodally distributed (a fast-growing low-ppGpp majority plus a slow-growing high-ppGpp minority, minority fraction ~10-25%), and upon an abrupt amino-acid downshift the seeds/lineages whose basal-phase ppgpp_conc trajectory shows the high-ppGpp tail have a significantly smaller post-shift growth_rate drop (shallower trough, ~>=30% smaller relative dip) than seeds lacking that tail.
select_score.h0: growth_rate and ppgpp_conc across seeds under constant basal media are unimodally distributed (no distinct slow/high-ppGpp subpopulation), and the magnitude of the growth_rate drop after an amino-acid downshift does not differ (|welch_t|<2) between seeds with high vs low pre-shift ppgpp_conc tails.

operational_defs.measure: Sarle's bimodality coefficient (BC) over pooled per-seed growth_rate values; BC>0.555 flags bimodal/two-state structure

falsifier.decision_rule: First, bimodality_bc on pooled per-seed growth_rate in wildtype/basal: reject bimodal-H1 if BC<=0.555 (unimodal). Second, welch_disconfirm comparing % growth_rate drop (trough vs pre-shift baseline) between high-ppgpp-tail seeds and low-ppgpp-tail seeds within amino_acid_shift design: reject H1 if |welch_t|<2 (no protective difference).
falsifier.refuting_result: growth_rate distribution across wildtype/basal seeds is unimodal (BC<=0.555, no slow/high-ppGpp minority), OR the % growth_rate drop after downshift does not differ between high- and low- pre-shift-ppGpp seeds (|welch_t|<2), showing no adaptive benefit to the heterogeneity.

rivals.claim: No heterogeneity exists: growth_rate/ppgpp_conc are unimodal in basal media, and all cells respond identically to the downshift (pure homogeneous population, no bet-hedging).
rivals.distinguishing_result: bimodality_bc on wildtype/basal growth_rate returns BC<=0.555, and per-seed ppgpp_conc traces show no distinct high tail -> H1 falsified at the distribution step.

rivals.claim: Heterogeneity exists but is a non-adaptive side-effect of stochastic ribosome/tRNA charging noise (intrinsic noise rival): high-ppGpp cells are just slower, not 'prepared', and show no differential benefit upon downshift.
rivals.distinguishing_result: bimodal distribution confirmed (BC>0.555) but welch_t on % growth_rate drop between high- and low-ppGpp-tail seeds is not significant (|t|<2) -> heterogeneity is real but not protective, falsifying the adaptive claim specifically.

rivals.claim: Any apparent protection is driven by constitutive ppGpp level differences unrelated to RelA-mediated stringent response (e.g. basal metabolic rate differences), so ablating RelA synthesis should not remove the protective correlation.
rivals.distinguishing_result: relA gene_knockout control: if the protective effect (smaller growth_rate drop in formerly-high-ppGpp lineages) persists despite relA knockout eliminating stringent ppGpp spikes, the mechanism is not ppGpp-dependent, undermining the stringent-response interpretation even if the correlational result in WT holds.

hypothesis.question: Can it ever help a population for some cells to grow slowly or stay 'prepared' for a change?
hypothesis.claim: Bet-hedging via stringent-response 'preparedness': a subpopulation of cells that constitutively maintain elevated ppGpp (and thus slower growth, higher RelA, lower ribosome content) under steady nutrient-rich conditions pays an immediate growth-rate cost but confers a population-level advantage when an abrupt amino-acid downshift occurs, because these cells show smaller growth-rate collapse and faster division-rate recovery than a population lacking this heterogeneity (i.e., a population with ppGpp clamped uniformly low).
hypothesis.h1: In an amino-acid downshift timeline, a wildtype population (which carries intrinsic cell-to-cell ppGpp/growth-rate heterogeneity) shows a smaller drop in mean growth_rate and a higher post-shift division_rate than a population with ppGpp clamped to a low, uniform level (ppgpp_conc clamp at 0.3x basal), even though the clamped-low population grows faster pre-shift.
hypothesis.h0: Pre-existing ppGpp/growth heterogeneity confers no population-level robustness advantage: wildtype and ppGpp-clamped-low populations show statistically indistinguishable growth_rate drop and division_rate recovery after the downshift (heterogeneity is selectively neutral noise, not a hedging strategy).

operational_defs.observable: ppgpp_conc and rela_conc distributions across seeds in steady pre-shift condition
operational_defs.measure: per-seed mean ppgpp_conc and rela_conc, CV across seeds (expect CV>=0.3 in wildtype vs near-0 in clamped)

operational_defs.observable: growth_rate channel pre-shift
operational_defs.measure: mean growth_rate in basal condition, wildtype vs ppgpp_conc=0.3x clamp

operational_defs.observable: growth_rate and division_rate channels across the amino-acid downshift timeline
operational_defs.measure: % drop in mean growth_rate at shift+1 generation, and division_rate fraction averaged over 2 generations post-shift

hypothesis.predicted_effect: Pre-shift: ppgpp_conc=0.3x clamp grows ~15-25% faster than wildtype (growth_rate higher by ~0.15-0.25 1/h). Post-downshift: wildtype shows a smaller relative growth_rate collapse (~20-30% drop) vs clamped-low (~50-60% drop), and wildtype division_rate recovers to >=0.8 within 2 generations vs <=0.5 for clamped-low — a qualitative crossover (hedging population wins fitness-integrated-over-shock despite lower pre-shift rate).

falsifier.decision_rule: Welch t-test of post-shift growth_rate (mean over generations 1-2 after shift) between ppgpp_conc=0.3x-clamp/downshift and wildtype/downshift across seeds; reject H0 (support H1) if |t|>=2 AND effect direction shows clamp population has LOWER post-shift growth_rate than wildtype. H0 (null hedging benefit) stands if |t|<2 or clamp population shows equal/higher post-shift growth_rate.
falsifier.refuting_result: If ppgpp_conc=0.3x-clamp/downshift shows growth_rate post-shift statistically indistinguishable from (or higher than) wildtype/downshift (|t|<2, or clamp mean >= wildtype mean), this refutes H1 — heterogeneity confers no robustness benefit.

test.statistic: welch_t
test.threshold: |t|>=2, with clamp mean growth_rate < wildtype mean growth_rate

rivals.claim: Rival A: Any slower baseline growth (not specifically ppGpp-mediated heterogeneity) buffers shocks equally well, i.e. the benefit is a generic growth-rate-vs-robustness tradeoff unrelated to stringent-response machinery per se.
rivals.distinguishing_result: Test with rrna_operon_knockout/downshift (lowers growth via reduced ribosome capacity, NOT via ppGpp heterogeneity): if this control shows the SAME robustness benefit (smaller growth_rate drop, high division_rate recovery) as wildtype, that supports Rival A over the ppGpp-specific hedging claim; if rrna_operon_knockout instead crashes like the clamped-low population, that supports H1 (ppGpp machinery specifically, not just slow growth, is doing the work).

rivals.claim: Rival B: There is no true bet-hedging distribution; wildtype 'heterogeneity' is just higher per-seed variance/noise with no mean-shifted adaptive subpopulation, and any apparent post-shift robustness is driven by mean ppGpp level rather than any bimodal/heterogeneous structure.
rivals.distinguishing_result: bimodality_bc test on pooled per-seed pre-shift ppgpp_conc values in wildtype: if BC<=0.555 (unimodal), supports Rival B (no distinct prepared subpopulation, just elevated mean/noise); if BC>0.555, supports a genuine bimodal hedging structure consistent with H1.

auxiliary_assumptions: The simulator's amino_acid_shift/timeline mechanism engages the stringent response (RelA activation) realistically enough that ppgpp_conc and growth_rate responses reflect the biological downshift phenomenon.

Per-seed variance in wildtype ppgpp_conc/growth_rate under isogenic steady conditions is an adequate proxy for 'cell-to-cell heterogeneity / bet-hedging subpopulations', even though the model may not explicitly simulate spatial subpopulation structure within one run.

A ppgpp_conc clamp at 0.3x basal is interpreted as 'population lacking preparedness heterogeneity' (forced uniformly low alarmone), not as a distinct mechanistic knockout; this is the closest in-envelope proxy for removing stringent-response-based hedging.
4 generations is sufficient to capture both the acute shock (gen 1) and partial recovery (gen 2-4) dynamics; longer-term evolutionary fitness integration is out of scope for this run.
division_rate <1 reliably flags a division defect distinguishable from pure growth-rate slowdown, allowing joint interpretation of both channels.
